synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
At a winter gala in Geneva, Declan Lincoln, thirty-one and the youngest chairman Lincoln Group has ever had, notices that the Thai idol sitting alone by the window is cold. Before she can say she’s fine, there is tea, and a cashmere shawl, and a man who asks for her number as if it were the simplest question in the world.

Cela Chanya, CC to everyone else, has never asked anyone for anything. Declan has never in his life waited to give. He buys her the garden when she would have been happy with one flower, and she says it’s too much, and then she smiles and says okay. Between Bangkok, Munich and New York, a mother with a suitable girl in mind, and a photographer who knew exactly where to stand, he courts her properly. Nobody else is allowed to know. Not yet.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
This is the soft one. A man who is very good at giving, a woman who is very bad at accepting, and the small, specific ways he gets round her: the water that isn’t cold, the soup at a six o’clock call, the butter tarts she mentioned once.

It’s still being written. New chapters come as they’re finished.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Never Asked, a Man Who Never Waited to Give
chapters.desc: At a winter gala in Geneva, the youngest chairman in Lincoln Group’s history notices that a Thai idol is cold and fixes it before she can say she’s fine. She leaves with his shawl, and puts a small heart next to her name in his phone.
chapters.epigraph: “Keep it. I’ll collect it when I take you to dinner.”
chapters.content:
By twenty-seven, Declan Lincoln had become a man people learned not to underestimate.

The youngest chairman and chief executive in the history of Lincoln Group, a multinational conglomerate with American roots and German headquarters, he had inherited the company at twenty-six following his father’s retirement. Some had questioned the decision. Others had waited for him to fail.

Neither group had been successful.

Within a year, Declan had restructured three major divisions, acquired two European technology firms, and expanded the group’s influence across the American and Asian markets. He had the kind of intelligence that made negotiations uncomfortable and the kind of composure that made it difficult to tell whether he was pleased or displeased.

At thirty-one, he was already a familiar face in the financial pages.

Tall, impeccably dressed, and almost offensively handsome, he possessed the sort of wealth that rarely needed announcing. His suits were tailored in Germany, his watches were rarely seen twice, and the private aircraft bearing his surname was considered one of the more modest luxuries in his possession.

He was generous, though not sentimental about it.

If he wanted something, he acquired it.

If someone mattered to him, he made sure they wanted for nothing.

It was a simple philosophy.

One that would become more complicated when he met Cela Chanya.

Or CC, as the rest of the world knew her.

At twenty-four, she was one of Thailand’s most recognisable international idols. Born in Canada to a Thai mother and Chinese father, CC had grown up between cultures, languages, and eventually, countries. She spoke English with a Canadian accent, Thai with the ease of a native, and Mandarin fluently enough to conduct interviews without a translator.

Her career had begun in Bangkok, but it had long since crossed borders.

Brand campaigns in Seoul. Magazine covers in Paris. Music releases that charted across Southeast Asia. Invitations to fashion weeks that most celebrities could only dream of attending.

She was beautiful in a way that didn’t demand attention but inevitably received it.

And despite her glamorous public image, CC was reserved in person.

Polite. Observant. Soft-spoken.

She smiled when necessary, laughed when genuinely amused, and had a habit of keeping her thoughts to herself.

She had sung one song for the foundation an hour earlier, a slow one, with a string quartet and a single spotlight, and that was the end of what anyone needed from her.

Which was why, at a quarter to midnight on the eighteenth of November, with the Lincoln Foundation’s winter gala winding down around her in a ballroom above the lake in Geneva, she was perfectly content sitting beside the panoramic windows, holding a glass of sparkling water while the rest of the room entertained itself.

Until a certain gentleman approached her.

“Miss Chanya.”

She looked up.

Declan Lincoln stood before her, one hand resting casually in his trouser pocket.

“Mr. Lincoln.”

“You’re familiar with me.”

CC blinked, then smiled politely.

“I believe your name is on almost everything in this building.”

He glanced around the ballroom.

A faint smile appeared.

“That’s unfortunate. I was hoping to make a more personal impression.”

CC laughed.

It wasn’t the response he had expected, but it was one he appreciated.

He took the empty seat beside her after a brief gesture of permission.

“I’ve seen your performances,” he said.

“Oh?”

“Several, actually. Including the one an hour ago.”

“That’s surprising.”

“Why?”

“I didn’t think you had much time for music.”

“I don’t.”

She turned towards him, amused.

“Then how did you manage several?”

“I have people who remind me to take breaks.”

CC laughed again, this time a little more genuinely.

Declan watched her.

There was something interesting about her. Perhaps it was the contrast between the polished celebrity everyone knew and the woman sitting beside him, who seemed entirely comfortable doing nothing in a room full of important people.

“Are you enjoying the evening?” he asked.

“Very much.”

“You’re sitting alone.”

“I’m enjoying that part, too.”

His mouth curved.

“Not particularly sociable?”

“Only when I have to be.”

“An unfortunate quality for someone in your profession.”

“Tell me about it.”

He laughed.

Their conversation continued for another ten minutes, moving from music to travel, from Switzerland’s weather to her upcoming schedule. She was more articulate than he had initially expected, with a quiet sense of humour that occasionally caught him off guard.

When a member of the event staff approached to ask whether she needed anything, Declan answered before she could.

“Something warm for Miss Chanya. Tea, perhaps?”

CC turned to him.

“Oh, no, it’s alright. I have my water.”

“You’re cold.”

She glanced down at her bare shoulders.

A champagne-coloured evening gown, delicate jewellery, and an open back that had looked more practical when she had left her hotel.

“I’m fine.”

Declan looked at the staff member.

“Please bring the tea.”

Then he turned back to her.

“Unless you’d prefer something else?”

CC stared at him for a second.

It was the way he did it.

Gently, and without any sign that he expected to be obeyed.

He noticed something, decided it could be made better, and made it happen.

“Tea is fine,” she conceded.

“Good.”

A few minutes later, the tea arrived.

So did a cashmere shawl.

CC looked at the folded fabric placed beside her.

Then at him.

“Mr. Lincoln.”

“Declan.”

She paused.

“Declan. I don’t think I need this.”

“You were cold.”

“I was managing.”

“Quite heroically, I imagine.”

She pressed her lips together.

He was smiling.

Not the polite smile he had worn throughout their introduction. This one was smaller, more amused, and accompanied by an expression that suggested he was thoroughly enjoying himself.

CC looked away first.

“You’re very generous.”

“I’ve been told.”

She carefully unfolded the shawl.

It was beautiful. Soft ivory cashmere, understated, with a small embroidered insignia near the edge.

She draped it over her shoulders.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome, CC.”

It was the first time he had called her by her stage name.

Somehow, she didn’t mind.

By twenty to one, the evening was over. CC stood near the entrance, waiting for her manager, who had been delayed by a conversation with one of the event organisers.

Declan appeared a moment later, his overcoat already on.

“Your car?”

“On its way.”

He glanced towards the glass doors.

“It’s snowing.”

She followed his gaze.

“Oh.”

“Your hotel?”

“The Four Seasons.”

“I know.”

She turned towards him.

He looked entirely unbothered.

“Your management arranged the accommodation through the event organisers,” he explained.

“Right.”

“My driver can take you.”

“That’s really alright. My manager is coming.”

“How long?”

She checked her phone.

“Perhaps fifteen minutes.”

Declan nodded.

“Then I’ll wait.”

CC met his eyes.

“You don’t have to.”

“I’m aware.”

He said it so naturally that she didn’t know how to argue.

A few moments passed.

“Do you always arrange things for people?” she asked.

“Only when I can.”

“That sounds expensive.”

His eyes returned to hers.

“Fortunately, I can afford it.”

She laughed, shaking her head.

There was something almost ridiculous about his confidence. Not arrogant, exactly. More like a man who had spent his entire life accustomed to solving problems before they became inconveniences.

Her manager eventually arrived, apologising profusely.

Declan exchanged a few words with him before turning back to CC.

“Goodnight, CC.”

“Goodnight, Declan.”

He paused.

“May I have your number?”

CC blinked.

It was so direct.

No elaborate excuse. No business card pretending to be a personal invitation.

Just a question.

“For what?” she asked, a little mischievously.

His face remained composed.

“To ask you to dinner.”

“Oh.”

“Unless you dislike dinner.”

“No, I like dinner.”

“That’s promising.”

She laughed and took his phone.

A moment later, his screen displayed a new contact.

CC ♡

Declan glanced at it.

The small heart caught his attention.

CC became interested in adjusting the shawl around her shoulders.

“Goodnight,” she repeated.

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

She froze for half a second.

He had said it so casually.

Then he stepped back, giving her a final, faint smile before walking towards his waiting car.

CC watched him leave.

Her manager leaned closer.

“Was that Declan Lincoln?”

“Yes.”

“Why does he have your number?”

She looked down at her phone.

A new message appeared.

Declan: You’ve forgotten something.

CC frowned and glanced at her shoulders.

The shawl.

Before she could reply, another message arrived.

Declan: Keep it. I’ll collect it when I take you to dinner.

She stared at the screen.

Then, despite herself, smiled.

CC: You’re very confident about getting that dinner.

His reply came almost immediately.

Declan: I am.

Declan: But I’ll still wait for your answer.

CC read the messages twice.

For someone who seemed capable of acquiring almost anything in the world, Declan Lincoln was surprisingly patient about one little dinner.

She tucked her phone into her evening bag.

And for the first time that night, she didn’t mind the snow.

chapters.title: Before Today’s Meeting
chapters.desc: Twelve hours off a plane from Geneva, CC learns the chairman behind her new campaign is the man with the shawl. He picks her up himself, backs her up in the meeting, and hands her a diamond bracelet with nothing attached.
chapters.epigraph: “Keep it, sweetheart. There’s no obligation attached.”
chapters.content:
Cela Chanya wasn’t fond of Monday mornings, and this one had begun at six, when her overnight flight from Geneva landed at Suvarnabhumi.

Not because she disliked working. In fact, she was disciplined about her schedule, rarely arriving late and almost never cancelling an appointment unless absolutely necessary.

She disliked mornings that began with people talking too much.

Unfortunately, today was one of those mornings.

“CC, are you listening?”

CC looked up from her phone.

Her manager, P’Nicha, was sitting across from her in the makeup room at AVEN ENT, holding a tablet with an expression that suggested she had already repeated herself several times.

“Yes.”

“What did I just say?”

CC blinked.

A pause.

“Something about the meeting?”

Nicha closed her eyes.

“Goodness.”

CC smiled apologetically and reached for her iced latte. Twelve hours in the air, and her body still thought it was somewhere over the Arabian Sea.

She was dressed in a simple white blouse tucked into a cream-coloured skirt, her hair falling loosely over her shoulders. There was little makeup on her face, save for a light tint on her lips and a touch of blush.

Five years ago she had debuted as one of the four members of BLUE HOUR, AVEN’s girl group, and for most of those five years her days had belonged to the group: rehearsals, stages, fan meetings, matching outfits. Lately the company had begun giving her days of her own.

Her schedule today was relatively light by her standards. A brand meeting in the afternoon, followed by a recording session and a short fitting for an upcoming magazine shoot.

The brand meeting, however, was the reason Nicha had been talking for the past fifteen minutes.

“Lincoln Group is one of the biggest investors behind this campaign,” Nicha explained again. “Their European division is handling the luxury partnership, and the chairman himself is attending today’s meeting.”

CC stirred her drink.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“Yes.”

“CC.”

“What?”

“Declan Lincoln.”

The spoon stopped moving.

CC looked up.

“Oh.”

Nicha stared at her.

“Oh? That’s all? Declan Lincoln, CC. The man who gave you his shawl in Geneva?”

CC’s expression changed slightly.

“It was cold.”

“And the man who sent flowers to your hotel the following morning?”

“He said they were from the foundation.”

“They were not from the foundation. They were from him.”

CC lowered her eyes to her drink.

A small smile threatened to appear.

Nicha noticed immediately.

“Oh, don’t smile.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

CC pressed her lips together.

Nicha sighed.

“Anyway, he’s attending the meeting today. So please, behave professionally.”

CC looked at her with mild disbelief.

“When have I not?”

“Last time you met a certain jewellery brand director, you accidentally told him his proposal was boring.”

“It was boring.”

“CC.”

“Alright, alright.”

She laughed and reached for her phone again.

There was a message from Declan, sent twenty minutes ago. She hadn’t changed his contact since Geneva. It still said Declan Lincoln, both names, like a business card.

Declan: Good morning, CC.

CC stared at it.

She hadn’t expected him to message her this early. In Bangkok, at least, he seemed to keep her hours.

CC: Good morning, Declan.

Three dots appeared almost immediately.

Declan: Have you had breakfast?

She tilted her head.

CC: Yes.

Declan: Proper breakfast?

CC smiled.

CC: What counts as proper?

Declan: Something other than coffee.

She looked down at the iced latte in her hand.

Then at the small plate of untouched pastries beside her.

CC: I had a croissant.

Declan: Excellent. I’ll inform my assistant that you’re sufficiently nourished.

CC laughed under her breath.

Nicha, who had been watching her, narrowed her eyes.

“Is that him?”

CC turned her phone face down.

“No.”

“CC.”

“Yes.”

Nicha leaned back in her chair.

“You’re smiling at your phone.”

“I’m allowed to smile.”

“Of course you are.”

CC picked up her latte again, trying hard to look unaffected.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Declan: I’ll see you at two.

CC: Looking forward to it.

She hesitated before sending another message.

CC: And you don’t have to send anyone anything today.

The reply took slightly longer.

Declan: I haven’t sent anything.

CC narrowed her eyes at the screen.

CC: Yet?

Declan: You’re learning.

She couldn’t help laughing.

A few kilometres away, on the thirty-second floor of the Lincoln Group’s Southeast Asia office, Declan Lincoln wasn’t enjoying his morning either.

He wasn’t a man who enjoyed unnecessary meetings.

He preferred concise reports, competent people, and decisions that could be made without three separate presentations.

His executive office in Bangkok reflected the same philosophy.

Floor-to-ceiling windows overlooked the city, the furniture was understated but expensive, and almost everything inside the room had been selected for its functionality rather than appearance.

Almost.

On his desk sat a small ivory box.

Beside it was a black folder containing the afternoon’s meeting documents.

His executive assistant, Alexander Weber, stood opposite him, reviewing the day’s schedule.

“The European team has confirmed the final numbers for the campaign,” Alexander reported. “The Thai management team will join remotely. Miss Chanya’s management will arrive at one forty-five.”

Declan signed a document.

“Good.”

“There’s also the matter of the Geneva foundation dinner. The communications department has requested approval for the photographs.”

“Send them to communications. Nothing with Miss Chanya unless her management approves.”

“Of course.”

Alexander glanced at the ivory box.

“Would you like me to arrange the delivery?”

Declan looked up.

“No.”

“Understood.”

“I’ll give it to her myself.”

Alexander nodded, making a note.

He had worked for Declan long enough to understand that there were certain matters in which his employer preferred personal involvement.

This was becoming one of them.

“Anything else?” Declan asked.

“Your father called this morning.”

That made him pause.

“What did he want?”

“He asked whether you’ll be at the family dinner in Munich on Saturday.”

Declan leaned back slightly.

“Tell him I’ll be there.”

“And he mentioned that your mother would like you to bring someone.”

Declan looked at him.

Alexander maintained a perfectly neutral expression.

“His exact words were that you should stop attending family dinners alone.”

A quiet laugh escaped Declan.

“My mother has too much free time.”

“Shall I tell her that?”

“No. I value my life.”

Alexander smiled.

Declan glanced at the ivory box again.

Inside was a delicate diamond bracelet from a private jewellery house in Geneva. He had seen it during a meeting with the designer two days ago and thought it would suit CC.

He hadn’t bought it because she needed it.

He had bought it because he imagined how it would look on her wrist.

There was a difference.

And, in his experience, the distinction was important.

“Alexander.”

“Yes, sir?”

“Have the car ready at one thirty.”

“Your meeting is here, sir.”

“I know.”

Declan closed the folder.

“I’ll be picking someone up.”

At half past one, CC was standing in front of the full-length mirror when Nicha came in.

“Your car is ready.”

“Okay.”

“Your lipstick.”

CC glanced at her reflection.

“What about it?”

“Touch it up.”

She looked at the soft rose colour on her lips.

“Why?”

“Because you’re meeting Declan Lincoln.”

CC turned around.

“I’m meeting the Lincoln Group representatives.”

“Of course.”

Nicha smiled.

CC gave her a look.

“You’re being strange today.”

“I’m simply observing.”

“Observe quietly, please.”

Nicha laughed.

CC picked up her handbag, checked her phone, and followed her manager out of the room.

She wasn’t nervous.

At least, she didn’t think she was.

It was that Declan had a peculiar effect on her composure. She was perfectly capable of holding conversations with executives, directors, politicians, and people more intimidating than a handsome billionaire.

Yet somehow, the thought of seeing him again made her conscious of insignificant things.

Whether her hair looked alright. Whether she had eaten enough.

Whether he would smile at her the way he had in Geneva.

She shook the thoughts away.

Ridiculous.

Downstairs, a black Mercedes-Maybach was already waiting at the kerb.

CC slowed her steps when she noticed the man standing beside it.

Declan was dressed in a charcoal-grey suit, a white shirt, and a dark tie. His jacket was unbuttoned, his watch glinting subtly beneath his cuff.

He looked as if he had stepped out of a financial magazine.

Which, considering his profession, wasn’t surprising.

But she hadn’t expected him to be here.

Her eyes met his.

Declan smiled.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

CC stopped in front of him.

“Hello.”

“Good afternoon.”

“Good afternoon.”

His gaze moved over her appearance.

“Beautiful.”

She blinked.

Then looked down at herself.

“Thank you.”

Declan opened the car door for her.

“Shall we?”

CC glanced at the car, then back at him.

“Weren’t we supposed to meet at your office?”

“We are.”

“Then why are you here?”

“To pick you up.”

“It isn’t on your way.”

“It is now.”

She gave him a small look.

He smiled, clearly familiar with that particular expression already.

“Come on, CC. It’s warm inside.”

She finally got into the car.

Declan followed, settling beside her.

As the door closed, he reached towards the small compartment between them and took out a bottle of water.

“Here.”

CC accepted it. It wasn’t cold. Every other car she had ever been put in kept its water ice-cold.

“It’s not chilled,” she said, surprised.

“You’re recording tonight.”

She stared at him. Cold water before singing tightened her throat. She had said so exactly once, in an interview, years ago.

“How do you know that?”

“I did some reading after Geneva.”

“Thank you,” she said, and found she meant it more than the water deserved.

“Did you have lunch?”

She turned her head slowly.

“Declan.”

“Yes?”

“Are you going to ask me that every time we meet?”

“Probably.”

She laughed.

“Why?”

“Because I suspect you’ll keep forgetting.”

“I don’t forget.”

“What did you have today?”

She paused.

A small smile appeared at the corner of his mouth.

“Exactly.”

“I had something.”

“Something?”

“Rice.”

“With?”

CC looked out the window.

He laughed.

“Alright. I’ll stop.” A few seconds later, he added, “For now.”

She turned back towards him, laughing.

He was impossible.

And, unfortunately, charming about it.

At three minutes past two, the meeting room was already full.

Several executives stood as Declan entered, greeting him with the usual formalities. CC followed a step behind, accompanied by Nicha.

Declan’s demeanour changed almost imperceptibly.

The warmth in his expression settled into something more composed. He greeted the executives, exchanged a few words with the European representatives, and took his seat at the head of the table.

It was fascinating to watch.

The man who had spent the car ride teasing her about lunch was now discussing international brand positioning and investment allocation with an almost unnerving precision.

CC sat beside her manager observing.

When the presentation began, she paid close attention.

She was there as the face of the campaign, but she wasn’t someone who liked being treated as a decorative addition to a business arrangement.

She asked questions about the campaign’s creative direction, the Asian market strategy, and how much creative freedom she would retain.

Declan listened without interrupting.

When one of the marketing directors gave a vague answer, he turned towards him.

“That’s not what she asked.”

The director straightened.

Declan rested his pen on the table.

“Miss Chanya wants to know whether the creative team will have actual authority over the final campaign direction, or whether the concept has already been decided by your department.”

A brief silence followed.

“Creative authority will remain with the appointed team, sir.”

“Then put that in the agreement.”

He turned back to CC.

“Anything else?”

She turned to him.

Then shook her head.

“No, that’s all.”

“Good.”

The meeting continued.

And for the next forty minutes, CC saw a different side of Declan Lincoln.

He was demanding, but never unnecessarily harsh. He expected people to know their work, and he had little patience for empty explanations. Yet he listened carefully when someone presented a sound argument.

He was young, certainly.

But there was nothing inexperienced about him.

When the meeting finally concluded, the executives began gathering their documents.

Declan remained seated, speaking with the European director.

CC was putting her phone into her handbag when a familiar voice came from beside her.

“CC.”

She looked up.

Declan had approached her.

“Yes?”

He held out the ivory box.

She looked at it.

Then at him.

“What’s that?”

“A small gift.”

CC didn’t take it immediately.

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“You’re saying my name as though I’ve done something wrong.”

“What is it?”

“Open it.”

She hesitated before accepting the box.

Inside was a delicate bracelet, its diamonds arranged in a fine, understated line.

It was beautiful.

Beautiful.

CC stared at it.

Then slowly closed the lid.

“Declan.”

He looked at her.

“I can’t accept this.”

“Why not?”

“It’s too much.”

“It’s a bracelet.”

“A very expensive bracelet.”

He considered that.

“Yes.”

She looked at him, slightly helpless.

He looked entirely pleased with himself.

“You’re impossible,” she murmured.

“I’ve heard that before.”

“From whom?”

“My mother, mostly.”

CC laughed despite herself.

Declan reached for the box again, but she held onto it.

He noticed.

A quiet amusement entered his eyes.

“Changed your mind?”

She pressed her lips together.

“I didn’t say that.”

“No?”

She looked down at the box.

Then back at him.

“You really shouldn’t keep buying me things.”

“Then stop looking so pretty when I see something I think you’d like.”

CC went quiet.

For a brief moment, she genuinely didn’t know what to say.

Declan smiled, lowering his voice slightly.

“Keep it, sweetheart. There’s no obligation attached.”

She held his gaze.

He wasn’t asking for anything.

Not a photograph, not a public appearance, not even a promise of another dinner.

He wanted her to have it.

And perhaps that was the most difficult part of refusing him.

Finally, she sighed.

“Okay.”

Declan’s smile widened a fraction.

“Okay?”

“Okay. Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She tucked the box carefully into her handbag.

Then, almost unconsciously, she added in a softer voice,

“But you really have to stop spoiling me.”

Declan looked down at her.

His face became thoughtful.

“That’s going to be difficult.”

CC laughed.

He offered his hand towards the door.

“Come on. I’ll have lunch arranged.”

She stared at him.

“Didn’t we just finish discussing lunch?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“And you’re coming with me.”

She tilted her head.

Then her lips curved into a small, resigned smile.

“Okay.”

Declan glanced at her.

She was wearing the small, resigned smile he had first seen in Geneva, over a cup of tea she hadn’t wanted. He had a feeling he was going to start collecting them.

And, judging by the way she had already slipped her hand into his offered arm, perhaps she was beginning to get used to him, too.

chapters.title: The Things He Didn’t Know
chapters.desc: Lunch at the St. Regis turns into an afternoon. He learns she apologises for small noises, speaks Mandarin when she’s tired, misses her father’s butter tarts, and keeps a separate stomach for dessert.
chapters.epigraph: “CC, we’re having lunch. You’re allowed to make noise.”
chapters.content:
The St. Regis kept a private dining room on one of its upper floors, with windows over Rajadamri Road and the green oval of the Royal Bangkok Sports Club below.

Declan had expected lunch to be relatively straightforward.

A pleasant meal, a little conversation, perhaps an opportunity to get to know CC beyond the carefully curated image that accompanied her public appearances.

He hadn’t, however, expected to discover that the woman sitting across from him was more interesting than he had anticipated.

“Do you come here often?” CC asked, looking around the private dining room.

“Occasionally.”

“It’s beautiful.”

The restaurant occupied a quiet corner of the hotel, with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the city. The table had been arranged with fresh white flowers, crystal glasses, and silver cutlery. There were only two place settings.

Declan pulled out her chair.

“Sit.”

“Thank you.”

He waited until she was comfortably seated before taking the chair opposite her.

A waiter approached with the menus.

Declan barely glanced at his.

“The usual for me. And for Miss Chanya...”

He looked towards her.

“What would you like?”

CC opened the menu.

“Can I have a little more time?”

“Of course.”

The waiter stepped away.

Declan watched her turn through the pages.

She seemed to take the menu quite seriously, occasionally pausing at a description before moving on.

“Anything you don’t eat?” he asked.

“Not really. I’m not very picky.”

“Allergic to anything?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She looked up.

“Are you always this thorough?”

“With people I’m having lunch with? Occasionally.”

CC smiled and returned to the menu.

A few moments later, she ordered a Thai dish, some vegetables, and a small portion of grilled fish.

Declan raised an eyebrow.

“That’s all?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“You can order more.”

“I know.”

“Then why aren’t you?”

“Because I don’t think I can finish more than this.”

He studied her before nodding.

“Alright.”

He didn’t insist.

That, she noticed, was nice.

Their food arrived shortly afterwards.

Declan had expected her to be somewhat reserved, perhaps even a little conscious of the fact that she was having lunch with a man she barely knew.

Instead, she was perfectly comfortable.

She thanked the staff, adjusted her napkin, and began eating.

For the first few minutes, their conversation revolved around work.

Her upcoming music release, the campaign discussed earlier, and the possibility of a European promotional tour.

Declan asked questions, occasionally making observations about the entertainment market that surprised her with their accuracy.

“You know quite a lot about the industry,” she remarked.

“I have investments in entertainment.”

“Music?”

“Among other things.”

CC nodded.

“That makes sense.”

He took a sip of water.

“What about you? Do you prefer performing or recording?”

She considered the question.

“Recording.”

“Really?”

“Yes. I like performing, but recording feels more personal.”

“How so?”

“When I’m performing, I’m thinking about the audience. The camera, the choreography, whether everyone can see properly. But when I’m recording, it’s just me and the music.”

She smiled.

“I can spend hours repeating the same line because I don’t like how it sounds.”

“Perfectionist?”

“Maybe.”

“Your producer must enjoy that.”

CC laughed.

“He complains about me quite often.”

“Does he?”

“Yes. He says I’m too particular.”

Declan leaned back.

“Sounds familiar.”

She studied his face.

“You’re particular, too?”

“Unfortunately.”

“Then I think you should understand him.”

He laughed.

It was an unexpectedly comfortable conversation.

Then, while reaching for her glass, CC accidentally knocked her spoon against the edge of her plate.

She caught it before it fell.

“Sorry.”

Declan glanced at the spoon.

“For what?”

“I made a noise.”

He looked at her for a second.

Then smiled.

“CC, we’re having lunch. You’re allowed to make noise.”

She laughed, a little embarrassed.

“Okay.”

He returned to his food.

But he remembered that.

She apologised for the smallest things.

The first unexpected discovery came when the waiter offered them dessert.

CC immediately read the menu.

Declan noticed.

“Thought you weren’t hungry.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re looking at the dessert menu rather enthusiastically for someone who’s full.”

She looked up.

A tiny smile appeared.

“I have a separate stomach.”

He laughed.

“Convenient.”

“It’s true.”

“What would you like?”

She examined the menu for another moment.

“Do they have mango sticky rice?”

The waiter confirmed that they did.

Her face brightened.

“Oh, I’ll have that.”

Declan met her eyes.

“Just one?”

She nodded.

“Would you like to share?”

CC paused.

“Do you like mango?”

“I have no objection to it.”

“Then we can share.”

The waiter took the order.

Declan watched her return to her water.

There was something amusing about the contrast. She had been so careful with her main course, but the moment dessert was mentioned, her interest had become more obvious.

“Do you have a sweet tooth?” he asked.

“A little.”

“A little?”

She smiled.

“Quite a lot, actually.”

He made a mental note.

When the dessert arrived, CC looked genuinely pleased.

She picked up her spoon, tasted a little, and hummed.

Declan watched her expression.

“Good?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

“That’s quite an endorsement.”

She scooped another bite.

Then, after a moment, she looked across the table.

“Do you want some?”

He glanced at the dessert.

“Go ahead.”

She tilted her head.

“I asked if you wanted some.”

He smiled.

“Yes, sweetheart. I’d like some.”

She pushed the plate slightly towards the middle.

Declan took a spoonful.

“Good?”

“Very.”

She smiled, apparently satisfied that he had approved.

It was a small thing.

But Declan was entertained by how naturally she had included him in something she liked.

The second discovery came through a phone call.

CC’s phone vibrated beside her handbag.

She glanced at the screen.

“Sorry, I need to take this.”

“Of course.”

She answered in Thai. Her mother, by the sound of it, had got to the phone first.

Declan continued reading something on his phone, not intending to listen.

But her voice changed.

It became softer, warmer, and more animated.

She spoke quickly, laughing at something the other person said before responding with an affectionate complaint.

Then she switched to Mandarin.

Declan looked up.

He understood some Mandarin, enough to follow a business conversation, though he wasn’t fluent.

Her pronunciation, however, was excellent.

She continued speaking for another minute before ending the call.

“Sorry about that.”

“Your family?”

CC nodded.

“My parents. My father, mostly.”

“He’s in Canada?”

“Markham. Just outside Toronto.”

Declan did the arithmetic. “It’s half past three in the morning there.”

“He has a bakery. He starts at four.” She smiled. “He called to tell me he watched Geneva on YouTube. Again. Fifth time.”

“A man of taste.”

“He makes the best butter tarts in Ontario. I’m not being biased. There was a newspaper.”

“What is a butter tart?”

CC put down her glass and looked at him as if he had confessed to something.

“You’ve never had a butter tart.”

“I’m beginning to feel I’ve missed something.”

“You have.” She sighed. “I miss them more than I miss the snow.”

He filed that away without comment.

“You speak Mandarin with him?”

“Usually. My mother speaks Thai with me, and my father speaks Chinese.”

Declan nodded.

“That’s how you learned both?”

“Mostly. I also studied Mandarin formally when I was younger.”

“Your Chinese is very good.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

He paused.

“Do you speak any other languages?”

“English, obviously. Thai, Mandarin. A little French.”

“A little?”

She laughed.

“Enough to order food and embarrass myself.”

“Useful skill.”

“Very useful.”

He smiled.

Then she added, almost casually,

“I actually prefer speaking Chinese when I’m tired.”

Declan looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t have to think as much about how I sound.”

She drank some water.

“Sometimes, when I’m working, I feel like I’m constantly adjusting myself. English for international interviews, Thai for local promotions, Chinese for Chinese media. I don’t mind it, but sometimes it’s nice to just speak without thinking.”

Declan understood that more than she probably realised.

He spent much of his life in rooms where every sentence was measured, every expression interpreted, and every decision scrutinised.

“Then you should do that more often,” he said.

Her eyes went to his.

“Speak Chinese?”

“Speak however you like.”

CC smiled.

It was a surprisingly thoughtful answer.

The third discovery was perhaps the most unexpected.

Declan had asked about her life in Thailand, assuming that she had spent most of her adult life surrounded by staff and professional assistance.

He wasn’t entirely wrong.

But there was something he hadn’t anticipated.

“Do you live alone?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“With your manager?”

“No, just me. My manager has her own apartment.”

“Do you cook?”

CC nodded.

“Sometimes.”

“Really?”

She looked mildly offended.

“Why does everyone look so surprised when I say that?”

“Because you’re a busy idol.”

“Busy people still need to eat.”

He smiled.

“Fair enough.”

“I can cook quite a few things.”

“Such as?”

“Congee. Noodles. Some Thai dishes. Chinese soup.”

“That’s quite a list.”

She looked pleased.

Then, as if remembering something, she added,

“But I don’t really like cooking for other people.”

Declan raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because they watch.”

He laughed.

“People watch you cook?”

“Yes. And then they comment.”

“On what?”

“Everything. Too much salt, not enough salt, why are you cutting it like that...”

She imitated someone else’s voice with a perfectly straight expression.

Declan laughed more openly.

“Sounds exhausting.”

“It is.”

“Perhaps you need a better audience.”

CC lifted her eyes to his.

He took another sip of water.

“I don’t comment on cooking.”

“How do I know?”

“You can test that theory.”

She smiled.

“You’re volunteering?”

“Naturally.”

There was a brief pause.

Then she looked down at her plate.

“Maybe.”

Declan’s expression softened.

He hadn’t expected her to entertain the suggestion so easily.

And he certainly hadn’t expected to find himself wondering what she would look like in a kitchen, wearing an oversized shirt, concentrating on a pot of soup.

An absurdly domestic thought.

He decided not to examine it too closely.

By now, lunch had extended beyond the time Declan had originally allocated.

His assistant had sent two messages.

He had ignored both.

CC, meanwhile, was carefully folding the napkin beside her plate.

“Do you have another meeting?” she asked.

“Not immediately.”

“You can go if you need to.”

“I’m aware.”

She looked at him.

He smiled.

“You keep trying to send me away.”

“I’m not!”

“You’ve asked me twice whether I have somewhere to be.”

“Because I don’t want to disturb your schedule.”

“You’re not disturbing anything.”

She gave him a smile.

Then her attention shifted towards the window.

Outside, Bangkok was moving through its usual afternoon chaos. Cars crawled along the road, the sunlight reflected off glass buildings, and the city looked busy from their quiet corner.

“Do you travel a lot?” she asked.

“Constantly.”

“Do you like it?”

“Some places.”

“What’s your favourite?”

Declan thought.

“Munich, perhaps. New York when I need things to move quickly. Switzerland when I want quiet.”

CC nodded.

“I like Switzerland.”

“Because of Geneva?”

“Partly.”

He watched her.

She smiled.

“The hotel was beautiful.”

“Only the hotel?”

She considered him.

Then looked away.

“Perhaps the company, too.”

Declan went still for half a second.

It was subtle, but he heard the implication.

A slow smile appeared.

“That’s good to know.”

CC picked up her glass.

She took a sip, hiding the small smile that had formed on her lips.

He decided not to tease her further.

Not yet.

When the waiter returned with the bill, Declan reached for it without looking.

CC noticed.

“Wait.”

He paused.

She glanced up at him.

“Let me pay for my part.”

“No.”

She blinked.

“Declan.”

He handed his card to the waiter.

“CC.”

“At least let me—”

“You’re my guest.”

“But we both ate.”

“And I invited you.”

She looked at him.

He gave her a calm, almost amused expression.

“Are we going to negotiate over lunch?”

She pressed her lips together.

“No.”

“Good.”

She laughed.

The waiter returned with the card.

Declan signed the receipt and stood, adjusting his jacket.

CC gathered her handbag.

As she stood, she noticed a little smudge of mango sticky rice near the corner of her mouth.

She reached for a tissue.

Declan noticed before she did.

“Wait.”

He took a clean napkin from the table and gestured towards her face.

“You have something here.”

CC instinctively touched the wrong side.

“Here?”

“No.”

She tried again.

He smiled.

“Other side.”

She looked up.

He was clearly enjoying himself.

“You’re not helping.”

“You’re doing wonderfully.”

She laughed, finally finding the spot.

“Got it?”

“Almost.”

She wiped it once more.

Declan nodded.

“Perfect.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She shook her head, smiling: a little resigned, a little amused, and softer than the smile she gave everyone else.

Declan walked her towards the private lift.

“Did you enjoy lunch?” he asked.

“Very much. Thank you.”

“Good.”

The lift doors opened.

They stepped inside.

CC watched him.

“Thank you for today.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And the bracelet.”

He glanced at her handbag.

“Have you decided whether you like it?”

She smiled.

“I haven’t tried it on yet.”

“Then I suppose I’ll have to wait.”

She laughed.

The lift stopped at the lobby.

As they stepped out, Declan turned towards her.

“Are you going back to the studio?”

“Yes. I have recording later.”

“At what time?”

“Six.”

He nodded.

“Then I’ll have my driver take you back.”

“You don’t have to. Nicha is waiting downstairs.”

“I know. I already arranged it with her. There’s a box of the mango sticky rice in the car for her as well. I gather she’s been waiting downstairs for an hour.”

CC stared at him.

“When?”

“While you were finishing your dessert.”

She looked genuinely surprised.

“You arranged that without telling me?”

“Would you have refused?”

She opened her mouth.

Then closed it.

Declan smiled.

“Exactly.”

She laughed, shaking her head.

“You’re really something.”

“Alexander says that too. He means it less kindly.”

They reached the entrance.

Her manager was already waiting outside.

Before she left, CC turned towards him.

“Goodbye, Declan.”

He looked down at her.

“Goodbye, sweetheart.”

She hesitated.

Then, with a smile, she added,

“Next time, I’ll choose the restaurant.”

Declan’s expression changed.

Not much.

Just enough for her to notice the immediate interest in his eyes.

“Next time?”

CC realised what she had said.

Her smile became slightly shy.

“Well...”

He leaned a fraction closer, his voice low and amused.

“I’d like that.”

She nodded.

“Okay. I’ll think about it.”

“Take your time.”

She turned to leave.

“CC.”

She looked back.

“Yes?”

“Try the bracelet tonight.”

She laughed.

“Why?”

“I’d like to know whether it fits.”

She shook her head, smiling as she walked towards her manager.

Declan watched until she was safely inside the car.

Only then did he retrieve his phone.

A message from Alexander was waiting.

Alexander: Sir, your four o’clock call has been moved to four thirty. The Munich team is ready whenever you are.

Declan typed a brief response.

Declan: Noted.

Then, after a moment, he opened CC’s contact.

He considered sending her a message.

Instead, he put his phone away.

He had learned quite a few things about her today.

She liked desserts more than she admitted. She spoke three languages fluently and became noticeably softer when speaking to her family. She cooked, apologised too often, and had a habit of looking pleased over the smallest things.

She was also more playful than her public image suggested.

And, most importantly, she had said next time.

For a man who usually preferred having every detail of his schedule decided in advance, Declan was quite willing to leave the next lunch entirely in her hands.

He suspected it would be worth the wait.

CC had barely settled into the back of the car when her phone vibrated.

Declan: I’ve just realised something.

She smiled.

CC: What?

Declan: I still don’t know what your favourite dessert is.

CC read the message, amused.

CC: Mango sticky rice.

Declan: That’s what you ordered today.

CC: Because I like it.

Declan: I see.

A moment later:

Declan: I’ll remember that.

CC stared at the screen.

Then typed:

CC: You don’t have to remember everything about me.

His reply came quickly.

Declan: I know.

Declan: I just want to.

CC read it twice.

She didn’t reply immediately.

Instead, she leaned back against the seat, looking out at the passing city with a smile she couldn’t quite explain.

Then she opened her handbag.

The ivory box was still there.

She took it out, carefully opened the lid, and looked at the bracelet again.

After a moment, she took a picture of it.

CC: I’ll try it on tonight.

She sent the message.

Then, almost as an afterthought, added a small white heart.

Declan saw it while entering the lift to his office.

He smiled.

Alexander, walking beside him, glanced at his employer.

“Something amusing, sir?”

Declan locked his phone.

“Not particularly.”

But the smile remained.

Finishing work early had never appealed to him much. This afternoon, it did.

chapters.title: Before He Leaves
chapters.desc: He calls to say he’s flying to Munich, then calls again to tell her about the flight. At the house on Lake Starnberg, his mother is waiting with a folder and a photograph: Charlotte Weiss.
chapters.epigraph: “Do you usually tell people your flight schedule?”
chapters.content:
At twenty past seven that evening, Declan Lincoln was supposed to be on his way to Munich.

The plan had been simple: one day in Bangkok after Geneva for the regional investment meetings and the AVEN presentation, and a flight out tonight.

But an acquisition discussion had run long, a few other matters had needed his attention, and the flight now left at eight tomorrow morning.

Now, with most of the work settled, there was little reason for him to remain in Thailand.

His principal offices were in Munich and New York. Bangkok was merely one of the many places he visited for business, not somewhere he intended to establish a permanent routine.

Yet, as he sat behind his desk reviewing tomorrow’s flight arrangements, he was reluctant to leave.

His phone was beside his laptop.

There had been no messages from CC since their afternoon conversation.

He glanced at it once.

Then returned to his documents.

A minute later, he picked it up again.

Declan exhaled.

This was becoming ridiculous.

He had spent most of his adult life travelling between continents, sometimes attending meetings in three different time zones within a single day. He had never minded leaving a city.

It was a matter of moving on to the next responsibility.

But now, he had a inconvenient thought.

He hadn’t told CC he was leaving.

He opened their conversation.

Declan: Are you finished recording?

He sent the message and returned to his laptop.

The reply came four minutes later.

CC: Almost. We’re just listening to the final version.

Declan: Have you eaten?

CC: Yes :)

Declan: Proper dinner?

CC: Yes, Declan.

He smiled.

Declan: I’ll take your word for it.

He put his phone down.

A moment later, he picked it up again.

Declan: Can I call you?

CC: Sure.

Declan pressed the call button.

CC was sitting on the sofa in the recording studio’s lounge when her phone began ringing.

She glanced at the screen.

A smile appeared before she even answered.

“Hello?”

“Hello, sweetheart.”

His voice sounded different over the phone. Lower, perhaps, and a little more relaxed.

“Hi.”

“Have I interrupted anything?”

“No. We’re taking a break.”

“Good.”

She tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Are you still at the office?”

“Yes.”

“You’re working late.”

“So are you.”

“That’s different. I’m recording.”

“Ah. My mistake.”

She laughed.

Declan leaned back in his chair, looking at the city lights beyond his office windows.

“How was the rest of your day?”

“Good. We finished the recording earlier than expected.”

“Did you like the final version?”

“Very much.”

“Then I’m pleased.”

There was a comfortable pause.

CC played with the edge of her phone case.

“Did you call just to ask about my recording?”

“No.”

She waited.

“I’m leaving Bangkok tomorrow.”

Her fingers stopped moving.

“Oh.”

“Early morning flight.”

“Where to?”

“Munich.”

“Germany?”

“Yes. I have several meetings there, and then I’ll be heading to New York later this week.”

CC nodded, although he couldn’t see her.

“That’s a lot of travelling.”

“Comes with the job.”

“Do you prefer Germany or New York?”

“Germany, when I want to work. New York, when I want to work without sleeping.”

She laughed.

“That sounds terrible.”

“It can be.”

“How long will you be away?”

“At least two weeks. Possibly longer, depending on the board meetings.”

“Oh.”

It was a small sound.

Almost insignificant.

But Declan heard it.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“CC.”

She smiled.

“What?”

“You sound disappointed.”

CC looked down at her lap.

“I’m not.”

“Not even a little?”

She hesitated.

Then, in a quieter voice, admitted,

“Maybe a little.”

Declan’s expression softened.

He hadn’t expected that.

Certainly not so soon.

“That’s rather nice to hear.”

She laughed.

“Don’t be too pleased with yourself.”

“I’m afraid it’s too late.”

He could practically picture her expression.

The slightly embarrassed smile, the way she would probably look away from the phone, and the little crease that appeared between her eyebrows whenever she was trying to hide amusement.

“Will you come back to Thailand?” she asked.

“Of course. I have business here again next month.”

“That’s good.”

“Are you going to miss me?”

CC went quiet.

Declan smiled.

“That was a straightforward question.”

“You’re asking a rather difficult question.”

“Is it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t know what answer you want.”

He laughed.

“I didn’t say there was a correct answer.”

She bit back a smile.

Then, after a moment, she said,

“I think lunch was nice.”

Declan laughed.

“Just lunch?”

“And the dessert.”

“Of course. I should have known the mango sticky rice would be difficult to compete with.”

She giggled.

“Thank you for taking me.”

“You’re welcome, sweetheart.”

He glanced at the time.

“I should let you get back to work.”

“Okay.”

“Get some rest when you’re finished.”

“You too.”

“I’ll try.”

There was another brief pause.

Then CC spoke again.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Have a safe flight tomorrow.”

He smiled.

“Thank you, CC.”

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

He ended the call.

He remained still, looking at the phone in his hand.

Then he opened his calendar.

His next visit to Bangkok was scheduled for three weeks from now.

He considered moving it forward.

He decided against it.

There was no reason to rearrange an entire business schedule because he wanted to see a woman again.

At least, that was what he told himself.

At home, a little after nine, CC had just finished showering when her phone rang again.

She checked the screen.

Declan.

She picked it up, slightly amused.

“Hello?”

“Are you busy?”

“No. I’m getting ready for bed.”

“Good. I won’t keep you long.”

She sat on the edge of her bed, wearing a soft cotton pyjama set, her damp hair falling over one shoulder.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then?”

“I realised I hadn’t told you something.”

“What?”

“My flight is at eight tomorrow morning. I’ll probably be unavailable during the flight.”

CC smiled.

“Declan, I think that’s quite normal.”

“I thought I’d inform you.”

“Thank you for informing me.”

“You’re welcome.”

She laughed.

There was something strangely endearing about a man who could negotiate million-dollar deals without hesitation, yet felt the need to personally notify her that he would be boarding an aeroplane.

“Do you usually tell people your flight schedule?” she asked.

“Not everyone.”

“Then I’m special?”

He smiled.

“Would you like to be?”

CC went quiet.

She hadn’t expected him to turn the question around so easily.

“You’re very good at that.”

“At what?”

“Making people not know what to say.”

He laughed.

“I’ll take that as a compliment.”

She smiled, lying back against her pillows.

“Are you packed?”

“Mostly.”

“Mostly?”

“My assistant is handling the remaining arrangements.”

“Then you’re not packed.”

“That’s one interpretation.”

She laughed.

“Declan!”

“What?”

“You should pack your own things.”

“Why?”

“Because you might forget something.”

“I have someone whose entire job is to make sure I don’t.”

CC shook her head.

“You’re spoiled.”

There was a pause.

Then he laughed.

“That’s interesting coming from you.”

She immediately sat up.

“Me?”

“Should I remind you about the bracelet?”

CC looked towards the ivory box on her dressing table.

She had already tried the bracelet on earlier that evening.

It fitted perfectly.

She had even taken a photograph of it, although she hadn’t sent it to him yet.

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“Because you bought it.”

“And you accepted it.”

She pressed her lips together.

He sounded far too pleased.

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“You’re right.”

Declan smiled.

He liked that she could disagree with him without becoming uncomfortable.

“Goodnight, CC.”

“Goodnight.”

“And don’t stay up too late.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

She smiled.

“Promise.”

He ended the call.

CC put her phone down.

Then looked towards the bracelet again.

After a moment, she picked it up and wore it once more.

It was delicate, elegant, and beautiful.

She took a photograph of her wrist against the cream-coloured bedsheet.

Then sent it to him.

CC: It fits perfectly.

Declan was in the middle of reviewing an acquisition report when the notification appeared.

He opened it.

For a few seconds, he studied the photograph.

Then he typed.

Declan: Beautiful.

A second message followed.

Declan: The bracelet looks lovely too.

CC laughed.

CC: You bought it. You should know.

Declan: I know.

Declan: I just prefer seeing it on you.

She stared at the message.

Then, unable to think of anything clever to say, she sent a small heart.

Declan smiled at his phone.

It was enough.

At a quarter past seven the next morning, Declan was in the lounge of the private jet terminal at Don Mueang, reviewing the final briefing Alexander had prepared.

His flight was scheduled to depart in forty-five minutes.

He wore a dark navy travel suit, a white shirt without a tie, and a long black coat draped over the armrest beside him.

Alexander approached with a tablet.

“Sir, the Munich office has confirmed your arrival arrangements. Mr. Schneider will be meeting you at the terminal.”

“Good.”

“Your meeting with the supervisory board has been moved to Thursday morning.”

“Fine.”

Alexander scrolled through the remaining schedule.

“And your father has requested that you attend dinner on Saturday.”

Declan looked up.

“At the house?”

“No, sir. The private room in Lehel your parents always use.”

“Who’s attending?”

“The Weiss family. Mrs. Lincoln asked that it be just the two families.”

Declan nodded, returning to his briefing.

Alexander hesitated.

“There was another request.”

Declan looked at him again.

“Go on.”

“Mrs. Lincoln asked whether you’ve had a chance to review the profile she sent last week.”

Declan’s expression remained unchanged.

“Which profile?”

“The young lady she mentioned.”

He remembered.

His mother had sent him a photograph and a brief introduction to the daughter of one of their family’s long-standing acquaintances.

A perfectly respectable young woman.

Educated, well-connected, and apparently interested in meeting him.

Declan had glanced at the profile once before closing it.

“I haven’t.”

“Would you like me to retrieve it?”

“No.”

Alexander nodded.

“Understood.”

Declan took a sip of his coffee.

His mother had been making similar suggestions for nearly two years.

At first, it had been occasional remarks during family dinners. Then came introductions arranged through mutual acquaintances, invitations to private events, and increasingly transparent attempts to seat him beside eligible women.

He understood his parents’ intentions.

They weren’t unreasonable.

He was thirty-one, unmarried, and spent most of his life working. His mother had long believed that he needed someone who could accompany him through the demands of his position.

Someone from a similar background. Someone who understood the expectations surrounding the Lincoln family.

Someone appropriate.

Declan, however, had never been interested in treating marriage as another corporate arrangement.

“Anything else?” he asked.

Alexander shook his head.

“That’s all, sir.”

“Good.”

Declan checked his phone.

There was a message from CC.

CC: Good morning! Have a safe flight today ♡

He smiled.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

Declan: Just about to board.

CC: Don’t forget to sleep.

Declan: I’ll try.

CC: And eat properly.

Declan raised an eyebrow.

He laughed.

Declan: Are you taking over my responsibilities now?

CC: Someone has to.

He reread the message.

Then typed.

Declan: I’ll put it in the minutes.

CC: Have a good day, Declan.

Declan: You too, CC.

He put his phone away.

“Sir?”

Alexander was waiting beside the lounge entrance.

Declan stood, picked up his coat, and followed him towards the aircraft.

The Lincoln house stood on the western shore of Lake Starnberg, forty minutes south-west of Munich, on land the family had owned for three generations.

It wasn’t ostentatious from the outside, despite its considerable size. The architecture was traditional European, with pale stone walls, expansive gardens, and large windows overlooking the property.

Inside, however, everything reflected generations of wealth.

Original paintings, antique furniture, carefully maintained collections, and the sort of understated luxury that didn’t need to announce its price.

Declan had gone straight from the airport to the office and reached the house shortly before ten. He kept an apartment in the city, but his mother had asked him to stay at the lake this week, and arguing with her would have taken longer than the drive.

His mother was in the sitting room when he entered.

“Declan.”

He leaned down to kiss her cheek.

“Mother.”

She stepped back, looking him over.

“You’ve lost weight.”

“Hello to you too.”

She frowned.

“I’m serious.”

“I’ve been eating.”

“Coffee doesn’t count.”

He smiled.

“Apparently, everyone has become very concerned about my eating habits.”

His mother looked at him curiously.

“Everyone?”

“Alexander.”

She shook her head.

“That man works for you. He should be concerned.”

Declan laughed.

His father appeared from the adjoining study a moment later.

“You’re late.”

“Good evening to you too, Father.”

His father extended a hand.

Declan shook it before they exchanged a brief embrace.

“How was Bangkok?” his father asked.

“Productive. The regional team has finalised the investment structure.”

“Any complications?”

“Nothing significant.”

His father nodded approvingly.

They spoke for several minutes about the business before his mother interrupted.

“Enough about work. You’ve just arrived.”

Declan turned to her.

“Alright.”

“Have you eaten?”

He almost laughed.

“Yes, Mother.”

“Properly?”

He paused.

Then smiled.

“Yes.”

She seemed satisfied.

“Good. Come sit with me.”

Declan followed her into the sitting room.

On the coffee table sat a folder.

He recognised the photograph on top.

His face remained neutral.

His mother noticed his gaze.

“Ah. I was hoping we’d have time to discuss this.”

“Mother.”

“Just listen first.”

He took the chair opposite her.

She picked up the photograph.

“Her name is Charlotte Weiss. Her father has been a friend of your father’s for years. She’s just moved back from London, and she’ll be at dinner on Saturday.”

Declan listened without interruption.

“She’s very accomplished. She studied at Oxford, speaks several languages, and has been involved in her family’s foundation.”

“Sounds impressive.”

“She is.”

His mother smiled.

“I thought the two of you might get along.”

Declan leaned back.

“Based on what?”

“You’re both around the same age. You have similar backgrounds, similar responsibilities...”

“Mother.”

“What?”

“I’m not hiring a director.”

His father, who had just entered the room, laughed.

His mother gave him an exasperated look.

“Don’t be difficult.”

“I’m not.”

“Then at least meet her.”

Declan glanced at the photograph again.

He had no particular objection to meeting Charlotte Weiss.

But he also had no intention of encouraging his mother’s expectations.

“We’ll see.”

His mother sighed.

“That’s what you always say.”

“Because that’s usually my answer.”

His father settled into the chair beside his wife.

“Your mother simply wants to see you settled.”

“I know.”

“You’ve spent enough years building the company. There’s more to life than board meetings.”

Declan smiled.

“I’m aware.”

His mother watched him.

“Is there someone else?”

The question was casual.

Almost too casual.

Declan reached for his glass of water.

“No.”

It wasn’t entirely a lie.

There was no relationship.

No commitment.

Nothing his family needed to know about.

At least, not yet.

His mother studied his expression.

“Good. Then you should have no problem meeting Charlotte.”

Declan reached for his water.

“We’ll see, Mother.”

She shook her head, clearly unconvinced.

But she let the matter rest.

For now.

Upstairs, at eighteen minutes past eleven, Declan had just finished showering when his phone lit up.

A message from CC.

CC: Are you in Germany already?

He checked the time and did the sum.

Declan: Why are you awake? It’s five in the morning there.

CC: Call time is six. Don’t say anything.

Declan: I wouldn’t dare. Yes. Just got back to the house.

CC: How was the flight?

Declan: Long.

CC: Did you sleep?

Declan: A little.

CC: That’s not enough.

He laughed.

Declan: You’re very strict.

CC: I’m the only one who says it to your face.

Declan sat on the edge of his bed.

He looked towards the window, where the Munich night stretched beyond the glass.

Then he typed.

Declan: Had dinner with my parents tonight.

CC: Oh! How was it?

Declan: Good. My mother complained that I work too much.

CC: She’s right.

He smiled.

Declan: You’re taking her side?

CC: I don’t know her, but I think she’s right.

Declan: Betrayed already.

CC sent a laughing sticker.

He looked at it.

Then another thought occurred to him.

Declan: What did you do yesterday, after the recording?

CC: Nothing! I slept. But Pim is making me go for hotpot tonight after the shoot. She says I’ve been “mysterious”.

Declan: Hotpot?

CC: Yes. It’s going to be really good.

Declan: Without me?

CC laughed at her phone.

CC: You weren’t here!

Declan: I see.

CC: I’ll invite you next time.

Declan smiled.

Declan: I’ll hold you to that.

There was a short pause.

Then another message appeared.

CC: Are you very tired?

He glanced at the screen.

Declan: A little.

CC: Then go to sleep. I have to go and be pretty for a camera.

Declan leaned back against the headboard.

Declan: Alright.

Declan: Goodnight, sweetheart.

CC: Goodnight, Declan. Sleep well ♡

He was about to put the phone down. Instead, he opened a different conversation.

Declan: Find out where AVEN’s six o’clock shoot is. Something hot for the whole crew by seven. No name on it.

Alexander: It’s eleven at night, sir.

Declan: In Munich.

Alexander: Understood.

He placed the phone on the bedside table.

For a while, he looked at the ceiling.

His mother’s words returned to his mind.

Charlotte Weiss.

A perfectly suitable introduction.

He had no reason to be concerned about it.

Yet his thoughts wandered elsewhere.

To a girl in Bangkok who liked mango sticky rice, spoke Mandarin when she was tired, and had apparently appointed herself responsible for reminding him to eat and sleep.

Declan smiled to himself.

He reached for his phone one last time.

He opened their conversation and looked at her profile picture.

Then he put it away.

There was no need to rush anything.

He would be back in Bangkok soon enough.

He was already looking forward to going back, and the reasons had little to do with business.

chapters.title: The Unusual Silence
chapters.desc: His mother can’t stop talking about Charlotte, and Declan takes it out on the office. CC doesn’t know why he’s quiet. She calls anyway, and sends a photograph of strawberries.
chapters.epigraph: “See? You sound happy now.”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln wasn’t an irritable man.

He was, by most people’s standards, remarkably difficult to provoke.

He didn’t raise his voice when negotiations went poorly. He didn’t slam doors when someone made a mistake, nor did he indulge in unnecessary displays of frustration. He had a reputation for being composed, occasionally intimidating, and almost annoyingly rational.

Even when displeased, Declan rarely showed it.

He became quieter.

And people who had worked with him long enough knew that his silence was worse than an outburst.

This morning, his patience had run out before he reached the office. It had gone at breakfast.

Breakfast at the lake house was at seven, in the room that looked over the water, and his mother had been waiting for him with coffee and a plan.

“Charlotte rides,” she said, before he had sat down. “Did you know? Dressage. She was very good at school.”

“I didn’t know.”

“She asked whether you still sail.”

Declan unfolded his napkin. “Did she.”

“And she speaks Italian. Her mother says she reads it for pleasure.”

“Mother.”

“I’m only making conversation.”

“You’ve made it about Charlotte three times since I came downstairs.”

“Twice.”

“The sailing counts.”

Behind his newspaper, his father made a sound that might have been a cough.

Eleanor ignored them both. “I told her you’d show her the boathouse after dinner on Saturday. She’d love to see it.”

Declan put his cup down. “You told her what?”

“It’s a boathouse, darling, not a proposal.”

He finished his coffee in silence, which his mother took as agreement, and left ten minutes earlier than he needed to. On the drive into the city, his phone lit up with a message from her: Charlotte’s number, in case you’d like to say hello before Saturday. He didn’t say hello.

He arrived at the office in the kind of mood his staff had learned to recognise from the corridor.

At twenty past nine, he looked up from the proposal in front of him.

“Explain that again.”

The director of the European operations division straightened in his chair.

“Mr. Lincoln, the revised acquisition figures were based on the preliminary projections provided by the regional team. We only received the updated numbers yesterday afternoon.”

Declan looked down at the document.

“Yesterday afternoon.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And your team submitted the proposal this morning without verifying the revised figures?”

The man hesitated.

“We were working under a tight deadline.”

Declan slowly closed the folder.

“Then you should have requested an extension.”

The room went quiet.

Across the table, Alexander Weber glanced at his employer.

Declan wasn’t raising his voice. He wasn’t even looking angry.

That was the problem.

“I don’t expect everyone to work at the same pace,” Declan continued, his tone perfectly even. “But I do expect people to understand the work they’re presenting to me. If the numbers are incomplete, say so. If your team needs another day, ask for it. Don’t put something unfinished in front of me and expect me to make decisions based on it.”

“Understood, sir.”

“Good. Have the revised proposal on my desk by tomorrow morning.”

The director nodded.

Declan stood.

“Meeting adjourned.”

Everyone began gathering their documents.

No one attempted to make small talk.

Alexander followed Declan out of the room and into the private corridor.

“Would you like me to move your eleven o’clock call?”

“No.”

“Your father also requested a meeting this afternoon.”

“Put it on the schedule.”

“Certainly.”

Declan walked towards his office.

Alexander glanced at him.

“Anything else, sir?”

“No.”

The office door closed.

Alexander looked at it.

Then returned to his desk.

He had learned not to disturb Declan immediately after a meeting like that. It had been a real mistake, but on any other morning it would have earned a raised eyebrow and a new deadline, not a silence that made two directors stare at the table.

At a quarter to twelve, Declan was halfway through reviewing a contract when his phone vibrated.

He glanced at the screen.

A message from CC.

CC: Good afternoon from Bangkok!

He checked the time.

It was almost noon in Germany, and late afternoon in Thailand.

He replied.

Declan: Good afternoon, sweetheart.

CC: Have you eaten?

Declan glanced at the untouched coffee beside his laptop.

He hadn’t.

Declan: Not yet.

CC: Declan.

He smiled.

Declan: I’m working.

CC: That’s not an excuse.

He sat back.

For some reason, that made him feel slightly better.

Declan: I’ll have lunch shortly.

CC: Promise?

Declan: Promise.

A moment later, she sent him a photograph.

It was a picture of a small plate of food, apparently taken at a restaurant. There was a bowl of soup, some rice, and a few side dishes.

CC: Late lunch with P’Nicha. We’ve been shooting since six.

Declan looked at the photograph.

Declan: Looks good.

CC: It is! I think you’d like it.

Declan: I’ll have to try it when I’m back.

CC: You should.

CC: Also. Someone sent hot jok and ginger tea to the studio at seven this morning. Enough for the whole crew. The card just said “For the six o’clock call.”

Declan: How strange.

CC: Very strange.

Declan: Was it any good?

CC: The stylist cried a little.

Declan: I’ll pass that on to whoever sent it.

He was about to reply when another notification appeared.

A calendar reminder.

His father’s office.

He exhaled.

Declan: I have another meeting. Talk later?

CC: Okay. Don’t forget lunch.

Declan: I won’t.

He put the phone down.

Then, after a moment, he picked it up again and took in the photograph once more.

A small smile touched his mouth.

Alexander entered with a folder.

“Sir, your father is ready for you.”

Declan locked his phone.

“Let’s go.”

At a quarter past twelve, Declan’s father was waiting in his private office.

Richard Lincoln was a man who shared many similarities with his son. Composed, deliberate, and accustomed to getting things done without having to repeat himself.

The difference was that Richard had spent nearly four decades building the company Declan now managed.

He was still involved in major strategic decisions, although he had gradually stepped away from the daily operations.

“Sit down.”

Declan took the chair opposite him.

“What is it?”

Richard slid a document across the desk.

“The board has concerns about the American division’s latest expansion.”

Declan glanced through the report.

“They’ve already approved the expansion.”

“They approved the initial investment. They’re questioning the additional allocation.”

“Because they haven’t seen the updated projections.”

Richard raised an eyebrow.

“Have you?”

“Yesterday.”

“And?”

“Proceed.”

Richard leaned back.

“You’re certain?”

“Yes.”

There was a brief silence.

Richard studied his son.

“You’re in a rather unpleasant mood today.”

Declan looked up.

“Am I?”

“Your expression has been like that since breakfast.”

“Ask your wife.”

Richard laughed. “Charlotte?”

“She’s promised Charlotte the boathouse.”

“Ah.” His father had the grace to wince. “She means well.”

“She always means well. That’s what makes it so difficult to argue with.”

“Whatever happened to you being the most patient person in the room?”

“I still am.”

“Apparently not.”

Declan closed the document.

“Is there anything else?”

His father shook his head, amused.

“That’s all. Go back to work.”

Declan stood.

Before he reached the door, Richard spoke again.

“Saturday. Don’t forget dinner.”

“I remember.”

“And your mother has already invited Charlotte.”

Declan paused at the door.

“I had gathered.”

“Try to be pleasant.”

Declan looked over his shoulder.

“Am I usually unpleasant?”

Richard laughed.

“Go.”

Declan left without answering.

Alexander had arranged lunch in Declan’s office.

A light meal, nothing elaborate. Declan ate while reviewing a presentation, occasionally asking his assistant to clarify figures.

Everything was proceeding normally.

Until his phone rang.

Cela Chanya.

He glanced at the screen.

Then answered.

“Hello?”

“Declan?”

Her voice was bright.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“Are you busy?”

“A little.”

“Oh. Should I call later?”

“No. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing!”

He paused.

There was something about the way she said it that made him smile.

“Then why are you calling?”

“Because I wanted to.”

Declan stopped reading.

He looked at the phone.

A small, almost involuntary smile appeared.

“I see.”

“Is that alright?”

“More than alright.”

He settled back.

“How’s your day?”

“Good! We just finished a photoshoot. I’m waiting for my car.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes, Dad.”

Declan laughed.

It was a genuine laugh, one that Alexander, who happened to be standing nearby, noticed immediately.

CC giggled on the other end.

“See? You sound happy now.”

Declan’s smile remained.

“Was I not happy before?”

“Not really.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Interesting.”

“You’re welcome.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for your assessment.”

“You’re very welcome.”

There was a small pause.

Then she asked, casually,

“Did you have a bad day?”

Declan glanced towards his office window.

“Not particularly.”

“Really?”

“Why?”

“You sound a little tired.”

He considered that.

“Just a few matters at work.”

It wasn’t work. But my mother has found me a wife wasn’t a sentence he wanted to say to her over the phone.

“Important matters?”

“Nothing I can’t handle.”

CC hummed.

He could hear the faint background noise of people moving around her.

“Then don’t think about them too much.”

Declan smiled.

“That’s easier said than done.”

“I know.”

Another pause.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Are you smiling?”

He looked down at his desk.

“Why?”

“Because I can hear it.”

His face softened.

“Perhaps I am.”

CC giggled.

And just like that, the unpleasantness of his morning seemed less important.

When the call ended, Declan returned to his documents.

Alexander entered a few minutes later.

“Sir, the revised presentation is ready.”

“Leave it there.”

Alexander placed the folder on his desk.

He hesitated.

“May I ask something?”

Declan looked up.

“Go ahead.”

“You seem to be in a better mood.”

Declan glanced at him.

“Do I?”

“Yes, sir.”

A brief silence.

Then Declan returned to his laptop.

“That’s good.”

Alexander almost smiled.

He had no intention of asking who had called.

He already had a reasonable suspicion.

By ten to five, the afternoon had become less pleasant.

A disagreement between the legal and financial departments had delayed a major approval. The matter itself was manageable, but the fact that two senior directors had allowed it to escalate into a pointless argument was beginning to wear on Declan.

He stood beside the conference table, one hand resting against the back of his chair.

“Let me make this clear.”

Both directors went quiet.

“I don’t care which department initiated the delay. I don’t care whose responsibility it was to follow up. What I care about is that we have spent three days discussing something that should have been resolved in one.”

Neither man spoke.

Declan looked at the financial director.

“Send the revised figures directly to legal.”

Then towards the other.

“Review them by tomorrow. If there is a legitimate issue, bring it to me. Otherwise, approve the document.”

“Understood.”

“Good.”

He picked up his folder.

“And please, don’t schedule another meeting to discuss this.”

He left.

The directors exchanged glances.

Alexander followed behind him.

“Your next appointment is at five thirty.”

“Cancel it.”

“Sir?”

“Move it to tomorrow.”

Alexander checked the schedule.

“Of course.”

Declan entered his office and loosened his tie.

He wasn’t angry. He was tired of explaining things that should have been obvious. And at three o’clock his mother had sent him a photograph of Charlotte on a horse, with no message at all, which was somehow worse than a message.

He poured himself a glass of water.

His phone vibrated.

CC: Are you still working?

He checked the message.

Declan: Unfortunately.

CC: Aww.

He smiled.

CC: Poor Declan.

He stared at the screen.

Then laughed under his breath.

Declan: Poor Declan?

CC: Yes. Very poor.

Declan: I should be compensated for this.

CC: How?

He considered his answer.

Declan: You could keep me company.

A few seconds passed.

CC: I’m actually free now.

Declan read the message.

Declan: Are you?

CC: Yes. I just got home.

Declan: Can I call?

CC: Of course.

He pressed the call button.

“Hello!”

Her voice came through immediately.

Declan smiled.

“Hello.”

“You’re calling very quickly.”

“I was told you were free.”

CC laughed.

“I’m free, but I didn’t say I was waiting for you.”

“Ah.”

He leaned back against his chair.

“That’s disappointing.”

She giggled.

“You’re so dramatic.”

“Am I?”

“A little.”

He smiled.

“How was your photoshoot?”

“Good. We did a lot of looks today. I think there were about six outfits. And then Pim took me for hotpot and asked about you seven times.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That you’re a man I met at a gala.”

“That’s all?”

“And that someone sent soup to a photo studio at seven in the morning, which has nothing to do with anything.”

“Nothing at all.”

“Long day.”

“Yes. My feet hurt.”

“Why didn’t you wear comfortable shoes?”

“Because they wouldn’t match the outfits.”

“Then you should have brought another pair.”

“I did!”

“Good.”

She laughed.

“Why are you asking so many questions?”

“Making conversation.”

“You’re usually better at it.”

Declan went quiet.

Then he laughed.

“Am I being interviewed?”

“No. I’m just curious.”

“About what?”

“You’re a little different today.”

He glanced at the documents scattered across his desk.

“Different how?”

“You’re quieter.”

He smiled.

“Perhaps I’m tired.”

CC didn’t immediately respond.

Then, in a softer voice, she asked,

“Did something happen?”

Declan appreciated that she didn’t immediately insist on knowing everything.

He could have told her about the acquisition report, the directors, the board’s concerns, and the endless stream of decisions that had occupied his day.

Instead, he said,

“Work has been rather troublesome today.”

“Oh.”

“Nothing serious.”

“Still troublesome?”

“Very.”

She made a small sympathetic sound.

“Then you should take a break.”

“I’m taking one now.”

“Because of me?”

“Who else?”

CC laughed.

There was a little rustling sound on the other end.

Then she spoke again.

“Wait.”

Declan heard something being placed on a surface.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

“That sounds suspicious.”

“Just wait!”

He smiled.

A moment later, a photograph arrived.

It was a picture of a small plate of strawberries and sliced mango, arranged neatly on a white ceramic dish.

CC: Here. A little treat.

Declan studied the photograph.

Then at the phone.

He smiled.

“What’s this?”

“Fruit.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why are you asking?”

He laughed.

“Thank you, sweetheart.”

She sounded pleased.

“You’re welcome.”

He looked at the photograph again.

It was such a small gesture.

She wasn’t there to make his day easier. She couldn’t resolve the issues at work or take the responsibilities off his shoulders.

But she had thought of him.

And somehow, that was enough.

Their conversation continued.

CC told him about a funny incident during the photoshoot, when one of the stylists had accidentally brought two left shoes for a particular outfit.

Declan listened, occasionally asking questions.

She was animated when telling stories, using different voices to imitate the people involved.

At one point, she laughed so hard that she had to stop speaking.

Declan smiled all the way through.

“You’re laughing at me,” she accused.

“I’m listening.”

“You’re laughing.”

“I find the story amusing.”

“You’re supposed to sympathise with me.”

“Of course. Terrible experience.”

She laughed again.

He shook his head.

“You’re quite demanding, CC.”

She made a little sound of protest.

“I’m not!”

“Not at all.”

“Declan.”

“Yes, sweetheart?”
