“Does she have a favourite ornament?”

He considered the question.

“There is a small glass star that belonged to my grandmother. My father puts it on the top every year, and my mother tells him it’s crooked.”

CC smiled.

“That’s lovely.”

“It is.”

She glanced up at him.

“I’d like to see it.”

“You will.”

He said it, without turning it into a grand promise.

And somehow, that made her feel better.

At twenty past three, Declan’s phone rang.

Alexander.

He answered, speaking in English, his voice returning to its usual businesslike calm.

CC moved away slightly to give him privacy, though he caught her hand before she could stand.

“You don’t have to leave.”

She looked at him.

He gave her a small nod towards the sofa.

She settled back while he took the call.

The conversation concerned a document that required his approval before departure. Declan listened, asked two precise questions, and gave instructions about the revised version.

It lasted less than ten minutes.

When he finished, he placed the phone down.

“Sorry.”

She shook her head.

“It’s okay.”

“Everything is arranged.”

“Good.”

He glanced at the clock.

“We should leave in about forty minutes.”

She nodded.

The words settled between them.

Forty minutes.

She looked towards the window.

Then she looked back at him.

“Can we stay a little longer?”

Declan’s expression softened.

“Of course.”

He reached for her hand and drew her closer.

They remained there until the time came to leave.

The private jet terminal at Don Mueang was quiet in the way only expensive places were: a lounge with low sofas, a passport desk with no queue, and a wall of glass looking out onto the apron, where his jet stood with its stairs down.

Alexander had already seen to the luggage and was coordinating the last of the departure arrangements.

CC walked beside him, holding her handbag with both hands.

She had been quiet since they left the apartment.

Declan noticed, but he didn’t try to fill every silence.

By the passport desk, Alexander approached.

“Sir, everything is ready. Your documents are in the folder.”

“Thank you.”

“The crew would like you on board by half past six.”

Declan nodded.

“I’ll see you on board.”

Alexander looked at CC.

“Have a safe journey home, Miss Chanya.”

She smiled politely.

“Thank you, Alexander. Have a good evening.”

He gave Declan a final nod and stepped away.

Then, at last, they were alone.

Declan turned towards her.

“Come here.”

She stepped closer.

He took her handbag gently from her shoulder and placed it on the nearby seat. Then he held both her hands.

“It’s not a long goodbye.”

She nodded.

“It still counts.”

“I’ll call you when I land.”

“Okay.”

“And I’ll send you a message before boarding.”

“Okay.”

He studied her face.

“Are you all right?”

She gave him a smile.

“Yes.”

He didn’t look entirely convinced.

She took a breath.

“I’m just not very good at this part.”

His face softened.

“Neither am I.”

She looked up.

“You’ve travelled so much. Surely you’re used to it.”

“I’m used to leaving places.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“I’m not particularly used to leaving someone I want to stay with.”

Her eyes softened.

She looked as if she might say something, but the words didn’t come.

Instead, she stepped closer and wrapped her arms around him.

Declan held her immediately.

One hand rested against her upper back, the other at the back of her head. He lowered his cheek against her hair and held her without rushing.

CC closed her eyes.

She could smell his cologne, clean and familiar. She could feel the warmth of his chest beneath his suit jacket.

It was strange how quickly a person could become part of the ordinary things one looked forward to.

Breakfast.

Messages.

A hand reaching for hers.

Someone waiting at the end of a long day.

She had known him for only a relatively short time, but she had already begun to associate him with comfort.

And now he was leaving.

“I’ll miss you,” she whispered.

Declan’s arms tightened slightly.

“I’ll miss you too.”

She drew back just enough to look at him.

“Don’t forget to eat.”

A faint smile appeared on his face.

“That’s my line.”

“I borrowed it.”

“Then I’ll try.”

“And sleep.”

“I’ll do my best.”

“Don’t work too late.”

He looked at her with quiet amusement.

“Anything else?”

She considered it.

“Be careful.”

He nodded.

“I will.”

Then he leaned down and kissed her.

It was gentle at first, but neither of them seemed eager to end it. His hand rested against her cheek, and she held the front of his jacket.

When they parted, she remained close.

He brushed his thumb beneath her eye.

“You’re going to make this difficult.”

She let out a small laugh.

“I’m not doing anything.”

“Exactly.”

She smiled, but it didn’t quite reach her eyes.

Declan kissed her forehead.

Then he looked towards the departure area.

It was time.

At five, they walked to the glass doors that opened onto the apron.

Declan held her hand.

He had done this countless times before: passing through airports, exchanging brief farewells, leaving behind one city for another. Usually, he was already thinking about the next meeting, the next flight, the next decision.

Today, he was reluctant to look at the aircraft.

At the entrance, he stopped.

CC watched him.

“This is where I leave you?”

“Yes.”

He nodded.

Neither moved.

Then CC reached up and straightened his tie.

It was navy.

Of course it was.

Her fingers lingered at the knot.

“Your tie is crooked.”

“It was perfectly straight when I left the hotel.”

“Maybe you moved too much.”

“An unfortunate habit.”

She smiled.

Then she smoothed the front of his jacket.

“There.”

He looked down at her.

“Thank you.”

She took a breath.

“Go. You’ll be late.”

“I have time.”

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

He picked up his carry-on bag, then turned back towards her.

She was trying to smile.

He could tell.

“Take care of yourself, sweetheart.”

“I will.”

“Message me when you’re home.”

“I will.”

“And don’t forget to use the bookmark.”

She laughed.

“I won’t.”

He leaned down and kissed her one last time.

When he pulled away, she held his hand for another second before letting go.

“Go,” she whispered.

He nodded.

Then he stepped through the doors.

CC stayed where she was, watching him walk away.

He crossed the apron towards the jet without hurrying, the evening heat coming up off the concrete.

At the foot of the stairs, he turned.

She was still there, on the other side of the glass.

Their eyes met.

He lifted his hand slightly.

She returned the gesture.

Then he turned away again.

He went up the stairs. CC watched until the doorway was empty.

Only then did she let out the breath she hadn’t realised she was holding.

Her phone vibrated.

Declan: I’ve been on board for forty seconds and I already miss you.

She stared at the message.

A small, helpless smile appeared.

CC: You should focus on your flight.

Declan: I’m trying.

CC: Good.

A few seconds passed.

CC: I miss you too.

She put her phone away and walked towards the exit.

In the cabin, Declan checked his phone again.

He reread her message.

Then he glanced at the window. The terminal glass reflected the sky. He couldn’t see her.

Alexander, settling into the seat opposite, noticed.

“Everything all right, sir?”

Declan slipped his phone into his pocket.

“Yes.”

Alexander opened his tablet, then glanced at him.

“Would you like me to arrange a call with Munich while we wait?”

“In twenty minutes.”

“Certainly.”

Declan looked ahead.

Alexander hesitated, then asked, “Is there anything else you need?”

“No. Thank you.”

Declan looked out at the terminal again. He owned the aircraft and set its departure time, and he was wishing he had told the crew nine o’clock instead of seven.

CC sat in the back seat.

Bangkok moved past the window, familiar buildings and traffic lights blurring into the early evening.

Her handbag rested beside her.

She reached inside and found the ivory leather case.

She didn’t take the bookmark out of the book. She only opened the book to where it was and looked at the engraving.

Until soon.

She ran her thumb over them.

Her phone vibrated again.

Declan: Boarding soon.

CC: Okay. Have a safe flight.

Declan: I’ll call when I land.

CC: I’ll be waiting.

There was a pause.

Then:

Declan: I wish I could have stayed longer.

CC glanced at the screen.

She typed a reply, deleted it, then tried again.

CC: I know. But I’m glad you came.

Declan: So am I.

She looked out the window.

A moment later, she sent one more message.

CC: Thank you for these days.

Declan: Thank you for letting me be part of them.

Her eyes softened.

She put the phone down and leaned back against the seat.

Missing someone, she was learning, wasn’t wanting them every moment. It was feeling their absence in the places they had just been: the back seat, the sofa, the spot by the glass.

At twenty to seven, Declan was still holding his phone.

The captain had come back to say they were cleared for seven.

“Sir,” said Alexander, “they’re ready when you are.”

Declan nodded.

He checked his phone one final time.

No new message.

He knew she was probably on her way home.

He opened their conversation and typed.

Declan: I’m boarding now, sweetheart. I’ll see you soon.

He sent it.

Then, after a moment, he added:

Declan: And CC?

She replied almost immediately.

CC: Yes?

Declan: I looked back.

She stared at the message from the back seat of her car.

Then she smiled, her eyes growing a little warm.

CC: I saw.

Declan: I know.

CC: I told you not to.

Declan: You did.

CC: You didn’t listen.

Declan: Not that time.

She laughed.

Then she typed:

CC: Next time, I’ll come with you.

Declan read the message.

His face softened.

He looked towards the boarding gate, then back at the screen.

Declan: I’d like that very much.

He put his phone away.

The next time he turned round at an airport, he had decided, she would be walking beside him.

CC arrived home a little after seven.

She changed into comfortable clothes, washed her face, and put the book with the silver bookmark on her bedside table.

She opened their conversation.

There was no new message yet.

She knew the jet would be taxiing by now.

Still, she sent one last message.

CC: Goodnight in advance. I hope you have a comfortable flight.

Then she added:

CC: I miss you already.

In the aircraft, Declan was settling into his seat when his phone vibrated for the last time before take-off.

He read her message.

A quiet smile crossed his face.

He typed a reply.

Declan: I miss you too, sweetheart. More than I expected.

He placed his phone away.

Ten minutes later, Bangkok was a sheet of lights falling away beneath the wing, and Declan Lincoln wasn’t thinking about the city he was leaving behind.

He was thinking about the woman who had told him not to look back.

The woman he had looked back for anyway.

And the next time he came to Bangkok, he intended to stay long enough that saying goodbye wouldn’t be the first thing on either of their minds.

chapters.title: A Colour He Would Never Choose
chapters.desc: She orders him a plum tie under Nicha’s email and has it delivered to Alexander’s desk. On Christmas Eve at the lake, he wears it to dinner, and his mother notices first.
chapters.epigraph: “I set an alarm. Did you wear it?”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday afternoon, CC had been looking at ties for nearly forty minutes.

There were several open tabs on her laptop, a notebook beside her, and a cup of tea that had long since gone cold.

She had started with a simple intention: find something Declan might like.

Somehow, it had become more complicated.

She knew his usual colours. Navy, charcoal, black, white, the occasional muted blue. His wardrobe seemed to follow a particular philosophy: understated, elegant, and almost impossible to get wrong.

Which was precisely why she didn’t want to buy him another navy tie.

She clicked through a collection of silk ties from an established Italian menswear house.

Burgundy.

Too dark.

Forest green.

Possibly.

Champagne.

Rather beautiful, but perhaps too light.

Then she found it.

A deep, muted plum with a subtle woven pattern. Not purple in an obvious way, but somewhere between wine and aubergine. The colour changed slightly depending on the light, and the pattern was visible only when viewed closely.

CC leaned towards the screen.

“Oh.”

She opened the product details.

It was handmade silk, with a fine texture and a restrained finish. Elegant without being conventional.

She imagined Declan wearing it.

Then she imagined his expression when he discovered the colour.

A smile slowly appeared.

He would never choose it himself.

Which made her like it even more.

She added it to her cart.

Then she hesitated.

Perhaps she should buy a tie clip too.

She opened another tab, found a simple brushed silver tie bar, and considered it. But she didn’t want to turn a small gift into an entire collection.

One tie was enough.

She checked the delivery estimate. Munich, Friday the twenty-second. She couldn’t send it to his apartment without asking for the address, and asking would give everything away. So it went to Lincoln Group headquarters, for the attention of Alexander Weber, under Nicha’s email, because an order in CC’s name to the chairman of Lincoln Group was exactly the kind of thing that ended up online.

She placed the order.

After completing the payment, she leaned back in her chair, looking at the confirmation screen.

She felt strangely pleased with herself.

It was the first time she had bought something for Declan without him knowing.

And she was looking forward to surprising him.

A few minutes later, her phone vibrated. In Munich, it was just past nine in the morning.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

CC smiled.

CC: Good morning.

Declan: How is your day?

CC: Rehearsal at six. Until then, I’m shopping.

Declan: For what?

CC: That’s classified.

Declan: I have very good security clearance.

CC: Not for this.

She glanced at the laptop.

The order confirmation was still open.

CC: What are you doing today?

Declan: A meeting with the board, followed by a review with the finance team.

CC: Busy.

Declan: Manageable.

She smiled at his familiar answer.

CC: Don’t let the finance team bully you.

Declan: They wouldn’t dare.

CC: Good. Have a nice day.

Declan: You too, sweetheart.

She closed the conversation.

The surprise was officially underway.

The days passed with the familiar rhythm of two people learning how to maintain a relationship across different time zones.

Declan’s schedule in Munich was full. There were board meetings, year-end reviews, and several matters that had to be settled before the Christmas break.

CC, meanwhile, was occupied with rehearsals, recording, and promotional commitments.

They spoke every day.

Sometimes it was a video call lasting nearly an hour. Sometimes it was a few messages exchanged between meetings. Occasionally, one of them would send a photograph of something ordinary: a cup of coffee, a meal, the view from a window, or a beautiful evening sky.

On Wednesday evening, Declan sent her a photograph of Munich after snowfall. It was past midnight in Bangkok, and she was still up.

Declan: It’s getting colder.

CC: It looks beautiful.

Declan: Beautiful from indoors.

CC: Are you complaining?

Declan: Merely making an observation.

CC: Wear something warm.

Declan: Yes, sweetheart.

She sent him a picture of herself wearing a thick cardigan.

CC: I’m warm too.

Declan: I can see that.

CC: Good.

Declan: Although I would prefer to be the one keeping you warm.

CC stared at the message.

Then she put her phone down, smiling to herself.

It was becoming difficult to have a normal conversation with him.

Not that she wanted him to stop.

On Friday morning, at Lincoln Group headquarters, Alexander placed a folder on Declan’s desk.

“Your mother called this morning, sir.”

Declan continued reading the document in front of him.

“What did she want?”

“She asked whether you’ll be at the lake by tomorrow morning.”

“I will.”

“She also wanted to remind you that the Christmas tree still needs its final decorations.”

Declan looked up.

“Didn’t she finish that last weekend?”

“Apparently, there are still some ornaments she hasn’t decided where to place.”

He gave a quiet sigh.

“Of course.”

Alexander smiled.

“She also asked whether you had received your Christmas arrangements.”

“My what?”

“Your mother’s words, sir. I believe she has made arrangements for the family dinner.”

Declan closed the folder.

“Thank you, Alexander.”

The assistant nodded and was about to leave when Declan’s phone lit up.

A message from CC.

CC: Have you had lunch? It’s nearly six here and I’ve just remembered you exist.

He checked the time.

“Not yet.”

CC: Declan.

He smiled.

Alexander noticed.

“Something amusing, sir?”

“Nothing.”

He picked up his phone.

Declan: I’m about to.

CC: Good. I’m at an early dinner with Nicha.

A photograph followed: her plate, with a small dessert at the side.

CC: I think you’d like this.

He looked at it.

Declan: It looks good.

CC: I’ll take you there next time.

Declan: I’ll hold you to that.

He put the phone down.

Alexander glanced at the document in his hand.

“Shall I arrange the remaining meetings for tomorrow morning, sir?”

“Yes. I want to finish everything before Christmas Eve.”

“Certainly.”

Declan returned to his work.

That afternoon, a courier left a small box at reception for the attention of Alexander Weber. Alexander signed for it, read the name on the order, and put it in his desk drawer without a word.

On Saturday afternoon, CC was in the middle of a rehearsal when Nicha approached her with her phone.

“Your package has arrived.”

CC looked up.

“You read my emails?”

“They’re my emails. You put a parcel to Munich on my account.” Nicha turned the screen round. An email from Alexander Weber, sent at nine that morning, Munich time, with a photograph attached.

The box was elegant and understated, wrapped in dark green paper with a small cream ribbon, and her own card tucked under it. The boutique had written the card out from her message, word for word.

CC smiled.

“It’s there.”

“What’s there?”

“Nothing.”

Nicha looked at her.

“CC.”

She hesitated, then smiled.

“It’s a Christmas present.”

“For whom?”

CC looked at her manager.

Nicha’s expression changed.

“Oh.”

CC laughed.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re thinking something.”

“I’m thinking that someone has become very thoughtful.”

CC took the phone from her.

“It’s just a small gift.”

“Delivered to his assistant.”

“So he doesn’t find out.”

Nicha looked at her with genuine affection.

“That’s sweet.”

CC lowered her eyes, smiling.

“I hope he likes it.”

“I’m sure he will.”

She read Alexander’s email one more time. It is in my desk drawer, Miss Chanya. He has no idea. I will bring it to the house tomorrow afternoon.

Tomorrow afternoon.

Christmas Eve.

Exactly when she wanted it to.

That evening, CC was sitting on her bed during a video call with Declan. In Munich, it was three in the afternoon.

He was in his study at the family residence, wearing a white shirt with the sleeves buttoned and a dark waistcoat. Behind him, a bookshelf and a framed photograph were visible.

“You’re at the lake already?” she asked.

“Since this morning. My mother needed someone tall.”

“For what?”

“Garlands. Over the doors. Apparently my father can no longer be trusted on a ladder.”

She laughed.

He met her eyes.

“You seem pleased about something.”

CC blinked.

“Do I?”

“Yes.”

“Maybe I’m just happy to see you.”

“Maybe.”

He didn’t look entirely convinced.

She adjusted the pillow behind her.

“How has your day been?”

“Productive. My mother has been preparing for tomorrow.”

“Is the tree finished?”

“According to her, yes.”

“And your father?”

“Has been instructed to move the star.”

CC laughed.

“Again?”

“Apparently, it was slightly off-centre.”

She smiled.

“I wish I could see it.”

“I’ll send you a photograph tomorrow.”

“Please.”

He watched her expression.

“Would you like to see the house too?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll give you a proper tour.”

She looked delighted.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

She nodded.

Then, before she could think too much about it, she asked, “Do you have to dress formally tomorrow?”

“It’s a family dinner. A suit, most likely.”

“Will you wear a tie?”

He turned to her.

“Probably.”

“What colour?”

“Most likely navy.”

She pressed her lips together.

He noticed.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“CC.”

She smiled innocently.

“I was just curious.”

He leaned back slightly.

“Are you planning my outfit?”

“No.”

“Are you certain?”

“Very.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“All right.”

She changed the subject before he could investigate further.

After they ended the call, she read Alexander’s email again.

She hoped he would open it before dinner.

And she hoped, even more, that he would wear it.

On Christmas Eve, the Lincoln family residence was quieter than the city.

Set on Lake Starnberg, south of Munich, the house had been decorated for Christmas over the previous week. Warm lights framed the windows, evergreen arrangements stood along the entrance hall, and a large Christmas tree occupied the centre of the main hall.

It was, as Alexander had once described, an enthusiastic undertaking.

Eleanor Lincoln stood near the tree, adjusting a small ornament.

Richard sat in an armchair nearby, reading.

“Richard,” Eleanor said.

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Does this look better here?”

He studied the ornament.

“It looks fine.”

“Fine?”

“Yes.”

She sighed.

“You’re not helping.”

Richard lowered his newspaper.

“I thought you were finished.”

“I am finished. I’m only making a few adjustments.”

He smiled and returned to reading.

Declan entered the hall a moment later.

“Good afternoon.”

Eleanor turned.

“Darling.”

She approached and kissed his cheek, then held him at arm’s length.

“You look tired.”

“It’s been a busy week.”

“Then you should rest before dinner.”

Richard glanced over.

“Your mother has already planned where everyone will sit.”

Declan removed his coat.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Very,” Richard replied.

Eleanor gave her husband a look.

“Don’t listen to him.”

Declan smiled.

He was about to head upstairs when a staff member approached with a small package.

“Mr. Weber brought this for you, sir. He said he couldn’t stay.”

Declan looked at the box.

It was wrapped in dark green paper, with a cream ribbon and a small card attached.

His face changed.

“Thank you.”

He took it upstairs.

In his study, he placed the package on his desk.

There was no sender’s name on the outside, only his.

The card was printed in a boutique’s neat hand, but he knew whose words they were before he read them.

A smile appeared before he had even opened it.

He carefully untied the ribbon.

Inside was a dark green box containing a silk tie.

He lifted it out.

He looked at the colour.

Muted plum.

A shade he would never have selected for himself.

He turned it over, examining the subtle woven pattern.

Then he found the small card tucked beneath the tissue paper.

For someone who has given me so many lovely things.

I thought you should have something from me, too.

I know you usually choose navy, but I wanted to see you in something different.

I hope you like it.

Christmas looks beautiful in Munich. I wish I could see it with you.

— CC

Declan read it once.

Then again.

His thumb rested against the last line.

He sat down slowly, the tie still in his hands.

He had received countless gifts throughout his life. Expensive watches, rare objects, personalised pieces, things selected by people who knew what he owned and what he was expected to appreciate.

But this was different.

She had paid attention.

She had noticed something as insignificant as the colours he wore.

And she had chosen something not because it matched his usual preferences, but because she wanted to see him in it.

He took out his phone.

It was a quarter to nine in Bangkok.

Declan: Sweetheart.

A few seconds passed.

CC: Yes?

Declan: My gift arrived.

CC: It did?

Declan: It did.

CC: Did you open it?

Declan: I’m holding it now.

CC: Do you like it?

He looked at the tie again.

Declan: Very much.

CC: Really?

Declan: Really.

She sent a small smiling emoji.

CC: I wasn’t sure if the colour would be too different.

He smiled.

Declan: It is different.

A pause.

CC: Oh.

He could almost imagine her expression.

Declan: I meant that as a compliment.

CC: You’re making me nervous.

Declan: Don’t be. I like it.

CC: You promise?

Declan: I promise.

He took a photograph of the tie resting across his open palm and sent it to her.

Declan: Thank you, CC.

She replied almost immediately.

CC: You’re welcome.

Then:

CC: I hope you’ll wear it.

Declan looked at the tie.

He already knew his answer.

Declan: I will.

CC: Tonight?

Declan: Tonight.

There was a pause.

Then her reply appeared.

CC: Really?

Declan: You sent it for Christmas. It would be rather disappointing if I kept it in the box.

She sent a laughing emoji.

CC: I wanted to see it on you.

He smiled.

Declan: Then I’ll make sure you do.

At a quarter to seven, Eleanor noticed the tie almost immediately.

Declan had come downstairs wearing a charcoal suit, a crisp white shirt, and the muted plum tie.

He looked as composed as ever.

But the colour was unusual.

Not unpleasant. Quite the opposite, actually. It added warmth to an otherwise restrained outfit.

Eleanor looked at him.

“Declan.”

He turned.

“Yes, Mother?”

“That’s a lovely tie.”

“Thank you.”

“New?”

“Yes.”

She stepped closer, examining the fabric.

“I haven’t seen you wear that colour before.”

“Neither have I.”

Eleanor smiled.

“It’s very nice. Who chose it?”

Declan adjusted his cuff.

“CC.”

His mother paused.

Then her smile grew.

“CC?”

“Yes.”

Eleanor looked at the tie again.

“Did she send it to you?”

“For Christmas.”

“Oh.”

She looked genuinely pleased.

“That was thoughtful of her.”

Declan nodded.

“It was.”

Eleanor’s eyes moved to his face.

“You’re wearing it tonight.”

“I am.”

“Because she sent it?”

He looked at his mother.

“Because I like it.”

Eleanor gave him a knowing smile.

“Of course.”

Richard, who had just entered the hall, glanced at his son.

“That’s a new colour.”

Declan looked over.

“Apparently.”

Richard studied the tie.

“Looks good.”

“Thank you.”

Eleanor turned towards her husband.

“CC chose it.”

Richard’s expression softened slightly.

“Ah.”

He looked at Declan.

“Then I suppose you should wear it.”

Declan gave a faint smile.

“I intend to.”

Eleanor was quiet.

Then she asked, “How is she?”

“Busy. She has rehearsals and some recording commitments.”

“Has she seen the tree?”

“Not yet.”

“Then show her tonight.”

“I promised I would.”

“Good.”

She adjusted the lapel of his jacket, then stepped back to admire the tie once more.

“It’s a lovely colour.”

Declan smiled.

“I agree.”

The dinner was smaller than Eleanor’s original plans had suggested.

There were close relatives, a few longtime family friends, and the people who had remained part of the Lincoln family’s Christmas traditions for years.

The table was beautifully arranged, with candles, evergreen decorations, and a generous selection of food.

Declan sat beside his mother.

Throughout dinner, Eleanor occasionally glanced at his tie.

She was trying not to make it obvious.

Richard noticed.

“You keep looking at him.”

Eleanor lowered her voice.

“I’m looking at the tie.”

“Of course.”

“It’s a lovely gesture.”

Richard took a sip of wine.

“It is.”

Eleanor glanced at her son.

“Have you thanked her properly?”

Declan looked up.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

A moment later, she added, “You should tell her I like it.”

He smiled.

“I will.”

Eleanor seemed satisfied.

The conversation moved on to family matters, travel plans, and the usual Christmas discussions.

But later, when dinner was nearly finished, Eleanor leaned towards him.

“Declan?”

“Yes?”

“May I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Is she happy?”

He looked at his mother.

The question was simple, but he understood what she meant.

He thought of CC’s smile when she had opened her apartment door that first morning. The way she had leaned against him on the sofa. The way she had reached up and straightened his tie at the glass doors at Don Mueang.

“I think she is,” he said.

Eleanor nodded.

“And are you?”

He glanced down at the tie.

Then he looked at her.

“Yes.”

His mother smiled.

“I’m glad.”

She didn’t ask anything else.

And Declan appreciated that.

By a quarter past ten, the house had grown quieter.

Most of the guests had left, and Eleanor was still downstairs with Richard, arranging a few things for Christmas morning.

Declan sat at his desk, his jacket draped over the back of his chair.

He had loosened his tie but hadn’t taken it off.

His phone was beside him.

A message from CC had arrived.

CC: I set an alarm. Did you wear it?

He checked the time. A quarter past four in the morning in Bangkok.

Declan: You set an alarm for this?

CC: Yes. Did you?

Declan: I did.

CC: Can I see?

He took a photograph of himself in the study mirror, making sure the tie was visible.

He sent it.

A few seconds passed.

Then:

CC: Oh.

Declan smiled at the screen.

Declan: Is that a good oh?

CC: Very good.

Declan: I’m relieved.

CC: It looks so nice on you.

He took in the photograph again.

Declan: I think I’ll have to reconsider my wardrobe.

CC: Does that mean you’ll wear more colours?

Declan: Let’s not become too ambitious.

She sent a laughing emoji.

Then:

CC: I’m glad you like it.

He typed a reply.

Declan: I like that you chose it for me.

A pause.

CC: I wanted to give you something you wouldn’t buy yourself.

Declan: You succeeded.

CC: Was that a criticism?

Declan: Not at all.

He settled back.

Declan: It’s a beautiful tie. And I like knowing you picked it out, thought about it, and sent it all the way here.

She replied with a small heart.

Then another message appeared.

CC: Did your mother see it?

Declan smiled.

Declan: Immediately.

CC: What did she say?

Declan: She likes it.

CC: Really?

Declan: She asked who chose it. I told her you did.

CC: Oh no.

He laughed.

Declan: What?

CC: Now she’ll know I have opinions about your clothes.

Declan: I believe she already suspects you have opinions about most things.

CC laughed.

CC: That’s not true.

Declan: Of course not.

A moment later, he sent another message.

Declan: She said it was iftful of you.

CC stared at the screen.

Her face softened.

CC: Please tell her I said thank you.

Declan: I will.

Then:

Declan: She also asked me to show you the Christmas tree.

He stood, walked towards the doorway, and took his phone with him.

Declan: Give me a moment.

He entered the main hall.

The Christmas tree stood beneath the high ceiling, its branches covered in warm lights, glass ornaments, and little wooden figures. His grandmother’s glass star sat at the very top, slightly crooked.

He took a photograph.

Then another, showing the entire hall.

He sent both to CC.

Declan: As promised.

A few seconds later, her reply arrived.

CC: Declan…

He smiled.

CC: It’s beautiful.

Declan: My mother will be pleased to hear that.

CC: I love the little ornaments.

Declan: The wooden figures?

CC: Yes. And the star.

Declan: That belonged to my grandmother.

CC: I remember you telling me.

He studied the photograph again.

CC: It feels very warm. Like a real family Christmas.

He typed slowly.

Declan: It is.

Then:

Declan: I wish you were here to see it.

CC didn’t reply immediately.

When she did, her message was simple.

CC: I wish I were there too.

Declan stood in the quiet hall, looking at her words.

Then he typed:

Declan: Next Christmas, perhaps.

She sent a heart.

He smiled.

Past midnight, Declan returned to his study and removed the tie carefully.

He folded it neatly and placed it back in its box.

He didn’t want it getting creased.

Before going upstairs, he sent CC one final message.

Declan: Merry Christmas, sweetheart. Thank you for my gift. Now go back to sleep.

No reply came. He hoped that meant she had.

He placed his phone down.

He looked at the tie box.

It was an unusual colour.

One he would never have chosen.

He would wear it again. The colour had little to do with it.

And downstairs, Eleanor was still talking to Richard about how thoughtful CC’s gift had been.

She had noticed something else, too.

Her son had worn the tie all evening.

Not once had he complained about the colour.

Not once had he tried to change it.

In fact, when Richard had asked whether he liked it, Declan had answered without hesitation.

He liked it very much.

Eleanor smiled to herself.

Perhaps, she thought, her son was finally learning that not everything worth keeping had to be chosen by him.

Sometimes, it was enough to let someone else choose something for you.

Especially when that someone was CC.

chapters.title: A Little Closer, Even From Here
chapters.desc: She wakes to his midnight message and, later, a wooden girl from the Munich Christmas market. That evening, Eleanor Lincoln says hello on a video call.
chapters.epigraph: “For your first tree. I’ll bring the tree.”
chapters.content:
On Christmas morning, CC woke to a message from Declan, sent a little after midnight in Munich.

Declan: Merry Christmas, sweetheart. Thank you for my gift. Now go back to sleep.

She smiled sleepily at her phone. She had, eventually.

In Munich, it was a quarter past two in the morning. The six-hour difference had become something she was increasingly aware of. When she finished work, he was starting his. When she woke up, he was usually still asleep.

It wasn’t difficult to understand.

But she had begun to notice how much she liked waking up to his messages.

CC: Merry Christmas. You wore it to dinner, and I’ve looked at the photo eleven times.

She put the phone down. He wouldn’t see it for hours.

His reply came at a quarter past three in the afternoon, while Nicha was in her kitchen arguing with a packet of glass noodles.

Declan: Eleven is a very low number. I’ll send more.

Declan: Good morning. My mother made sure I went to bed at a reasonable hour, which she defines as after midnight.

A moment later, he sent a photograph.

It was the Christmas tree in the main hall, taken from a slightly different angle than the previous evening. Morning light filtered through the windows, illuminating the ornaments and the little glass star near the top.

CC smiled.

CC: It looks even prettier in the morning.

Declan: My mother will be pleased. She’s rather proud of it.

CC: I can understand why.

Declan: Lunch with my parents later. Then dinner with the family.

CC: Have a lovely day with them.

Declan: Thank you, sweetheart. What are your plans?

CC: Nicha’s here. We’re cooking, badly. My parents called this morning from their Christmas Eve.

Declan: Good. Don’t let Nicha talk about schedules.

CC: Too late.

He sent a small heart.

She put her phone face down on the counter, then turned it over to look at the photograph once more.

The house looked warm.

She imagined Declan there, walking through the hall in his dark clothes, his mother arranging the last few decorations, his father probably pretending not to be involved.

It made her smile.

She was glad he had sent the photograph.

It felt like being allowed a small glimpse into a part of his life she hadn’t seen yet.

Twenty minutes later, the concierge called up. A courier had left a box for her.

It was the size of her hand, packed in straw. Inside was a carved wooden figure no taller than her thumb: a small girl in a painted red coat, holding a gold star almost as big as she was. It was exactly like the little figures on the tree in the photograph.

The card was in his handwriting.

From the Christmas market at Marienplatz, on Wednesday, in the snow. For your first tree. I’ll bring the tree.

— D.

She read it twice, then looked around her living room, which had no tree, no lights, and one wooden girl standing on the coffee table.

CC: I have a figure and no tree.

Declan: That’s the idea.

Nicha came out of the kitchen, looked at the girl in the red coat, looked at CC’s face, and went back into the kitchen without saying a word.

At the lake, a little before noon, Eleanor Lincoln was in the kitchen when Declan came downstairs.

She was speaking with the cook about the afternoon meal, occasionally glancing at a handwritten list.

“Declan.”

He approached.

“Yes, Mother?”

“Could you take these to your father?”

She handed him a small plate of biscuits.

He had put the plum tie on again that morning. She had noticed, and said nothing, which for Eleanor was a considerable effort.

“And tell him not to eat too many before lunch.”

Declan glanced at the plate.

“I suspect he’s already had some.”

Eleanor gave him a knowing look.

“Then tell him I know.”

He smiled and left the kitchen.

Richard was in the adjoining sitting room, reading a newspaper beside the fireplace.

Declan placed the plate on the table.

“Mother says not to eat too many.”

Richard looked at the biscuits.

“How many is too many?”

“I didn’t ask.”

“Then I’ll have to determine that myself.”

Declan gave a quiet laugh and sat across from him.

Richard folded the newspaper.

“How is CC?”

Declan looked up.

“Your mother has mentioned her four times since breakfast,” Richard said. “I thought I should ask before she makes it five.”

“She’s well.”

Richard looked at the tie. “Twice in two days.”

“It’s a good tie.”

Richard looked at his son.

“You seem rather pleased with it.”

“I am.”

“Good.”

There was a brief silence.

Then Richard asked, “Will you speak to her today?”

“Later. We arranged a call.”

Richard nodded.

“Then I won’t keep you.”

Declan smiled slightly.

“I’m not in a hurry.”

But he glanced at his phone anyway.

Richard noticed.

He said nothing.

In Bangkok, CC had spent most of the afternoon with Nicha.

They had lunch, exchanged small Christmas gifts, and watched a film in the living room. Nicha had gone home a little earlier, leaving CC with a quiet evening.

She had changed into comfortable clothes and was sitting on her sofa, a little after eight, when her phone rang. In Munich, lunch would just be over.

Declan.

She answered immediately.

His face appeared on the screen.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

She smiled.

“Hi.”

He was sitting in what looked like a sitting room. The lighting was warm, and behind him she could see part of a fireplace and a tall bookshelf.

“You look comfortable,” he said.

“I am. How has your day been?”

“Very good. We had lunch, and my mother insisted on taking several photographs.”

CC laughed.

“Did you let her?”

“I had little choice.”

“I’m sure she wanted pictures of everyone.”

“She did. Including several of me that I suspect will be used against me in the future.”

She laughed again.

Declan smiled, watching her.

“What did you do today?”

“Nicha and I cooked, which was a mistake. Then we exchanged gifts and watched a movie.” She held the wooden girl up to the camera. “And someone sent me this.”

“Did she arrive in one piece?”

“She’s perfect. She’s standing on my coffee table, waiting for a tree.”

“She won’t wait long.”

She adjusted her position on the sofa.

“Was lunch good?”

“My mother prepared more food than anyone could reasonably eat.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“Does your mother do the same?”

“My mother does. She always thinks everyone is hungry.”

Declan smiled.

“Perhaps they would get along.”

CC laughed.

“Maybe.”

He glanced towards something outside the frame.

Then he looked back at her.

“My mother is here, actually.”

CC blinked.

“Oh?”

“She was asking who I was speaking to.”

Her fingers tightened slightly around the phone.

Declan noticed the small change in her expression.

“Would you like to say hello?”

She met his eyes.

“Now?”

“If you’re comfortable.”

She hesitated.

It wasn’t that she didn’t want to meet Eleanor. Quite the opposite. She had thought about it more than once since Declan told her his mother was curious about her.

But there was a difference between imagining a future introduction and having the opportunity to say hello.

“Is she nearby?”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

CC quickly looked at herself on the screen, smoothing her hair.

Declan’s expression turned amused.

“You look lovely.”

“Don’t.”

“I’m only telling the truth.”

She gave him a small look.

“Wait. Let me sit properly.”

He laughed.

“Take your time.”

Eleanor entered the sitting room carrying a cup of tea.

She had initially intended to ask Declan something about the following day’s arrangements, but when she noticed the video call on his phone, she stopped.

“Are you speaking to CC?”

Declan nodded.

“Yes.”

Eleanor smiled.

“May I say hello?”

He looked towards the screen.

“She’s here.”

CC gave a small, nervous smile.

Eleanor approached and sat beside her son, making sure she was visible.

“Hello, CC.”

CC sat a little straighter.

“Hello, Mrs. Lincoln.”

Eleanor’s smile warmed.

“Please, call me Eleanor.”

CC nodded.

“It’s very nice to meet you.”

“It’s lovely to meet you too.”

For a moment, CC wasn’t sure what to say next.

She had met many important people throughout her career. She had attended formal events, spoken to executives, and sat through interviews with people who asked questions far more difficult than this.

Yet somehow, greeting Declan’s mother made her more nervous than any of those occasions.

Eleanor seemed to understand.

“I hope we’re not interrupting your Christmas evening.”

“Oh, no. Not at all.”

“Good. Declan told me you were spending the day with your manager.”

“Yes. We tried to cook.”

“Tried?”

“We ordered in.”

Eleanor laughed.

Eleanor glanced at her son.

“He’s been telling us a little about you.”

CC’s eyes widened slightly.

“He has?”

Declan looked amused.

“Not very much.”

Eleanor gave him a look.

“Enough for me to know that you have been taking very good care of him.”

CC blinked.

Then she laughed.

“I don’t know about that.”

“Oh, I think you do.”

Declan leaned back, looking perfectly content to let his mother speak.

Eleanor continued, “He seems very happy lately. And I wanted to thank you for the lovely tie.”

CC’s cheeks warmed.

“I’m glad you liked it.”

“I did. It’s a beautiful colour. I thought it suited him very well.”

“Thank you. I wasn’t sure whether he would like it because he usually wears navy.”

Eleanor laughed.

“Oh, I noticed. He has a rather predictable wardrobe.”

Declan looked at his mother.

“Mother.”

“What? It’s true.”

CC laughed, and some of her nervousness disappeared.

Eleanor looked back at her.

“I thought it was very thoughtful of you to choose something different for him.”

“I wanted to give him something he wouldn’t usually buy for himself.”

“Well, you succeeded.”

Declan smiled.

“I believe we’ve established that.”

Eleanor’s expression softened.

“I’m glad you two are enjoying your time together.”

CC lowered her eyes.

“Thank you.”

There was a gentle pause.

Then Eleanor said, “I hope one day we’ll have the chance to meet properly. But there’s no hurry. I know you have a busy schedule.”

CC looked up.

“I’d like that very much.”

“Then we’ll leave it for another time.”

She smiled warmly.

“Merry Christmas, CC.”

“Merry Christmas, Eleanor.”

Eleanor stood.

“I’ll let you two talk. Declan, don’t keep her up too late.”

Declan looked at his mother.

“I won’t.”

“And don’t let him work tomorrow. He’ll try.”

“Mother.”

She smiled at CC.

“See? I still have to remind him.”

CC laughed.

“I’ll remind him too.”

Eleanor looked delighted.

“Excellent. Then perhaps I can finally retire from the responsibility.”

She gave her son a light touch on the shoulder before leaving the room.

Declan watched her go, then turned his attention back to the screen.

CC was still looking towards where his mother had disappeared.

He smiled.

“She’s gone.”

She looked back at him.

“That was your mother?”

He laughed.

“Yes.”

“She was so nice.”

“I told you she would be.”

CC smiled, still looking a little surprised.

“She really was.”

For a moment, CC didn’t say anything.

Declan watched her expression.

“What are you thinking?”

She turned to him.

“Nothing.”

“That’s rarely true.”

She smiled.

“I was just nervous.”

“I noticed.”

“Was it obvious?”

“A little.”

She covered her face.

“Oh, no.”

He laughed.

“Don’t worry. My mother thought you were lovely.”

CC lowered her hands.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“What has she said about me? Before today?”

Declan leaned back.

“That she hoped you were as kind as you sounded.”

CC blinked.

“As I sounded?”

“She has heard some of your music.”

CC’s expression changed.

“Oh.”

“She listened to your solo song after I showed her the video.”

CC looked down, smiling shyly.

“Did she like it?”

“She did.”

“Really?”

“She said your voice was beautiful.”

CC pressed her lips together.

She wasn’t accustomed to being shy about compliments. She could accept praise from producers, interviewers, and fans without much difficulty.

But hearing that Declan’s mother had listened to her song made her feel unexpectedly touched.

“That’s very kind of her.”

“I’ll tell her.”

She looked back at him.

“Please do.”

Declan studied her face.

“You seem happier now.”

She nodded.

“I am.”

“Good.”

She shifted slightly on the sofa.

“I was afraid she might think I’m too young for you.”

Declan’s expression changed.

“Why would you think that?”

“I don’t know. You’re older, and your family…”

She trailed off.

He understood.

“CC.”

She looked at him.

“My family doesn’t get to decide whether you’re right for me.”

She listened.

“And I don’t want you to feel that you have to prove anything to them. Or to me.”

Her face softened.

“Okay.”

“I chose to pursue you because I like you. Because I enjoy being with you. Not because you fit some expectation.”

She nodded.

“Thank you.”

He smiled.

“And for what it’s worth, my mother is far more interested in whether you’re happy than in how old you are.”

CC laughed.

“That’s reassuring.”

“Good.”

She leaned against the sofa cushion.

“Your mother is very pretty.”

Declan raised an eyebrow.

“Is she?”

“Yes. And she has a very warm smile.”

“I’ll tell her you said that.”

“Don’t. She’ll think I’m trying to flatter her.”

“Perhaps you are.”

She laughed.

“I’m not.”

He smiled.

They continued talking for a while.

CC asked about the lunch, the family photographs, and how many biscuits his father had eaten. Declan told her about a cousin who had arrived late and a family friend who had brought an enormous box of chocolates.

She listened with interest, occasionally asking questions.

It was the first time he had shared so much of his family Christmas with her in real time.

And he liked it.

CC had begun to relax completely.

She was lying on her side now, her phone propped against a cushion.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Did you tell your mother about the first time we met?”

“At the gala?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That I met a very lovely woman who was cold.”

CC laughed.

“That’s all?”

“I also told her I gave you my shawl.”

She smiled.

“Did you tell her you asked for my number?”

“Yes.”

“And that I gave it to you?”

“I did.”

She held his gaze.

“What did she say?”

“She asked whether you had been interested in me.”

CC’s eyes widened.

“Declan!”

He laughed.

“What?”

“You told her that?”

“Of course.”

“What did you say?”

“That I hoped you were.”

She covered her face again.

He smiled, clearly enjoying her reaction.

“She seemed rather pleased with the answer.”

CC lowered her hands.

“Your mother asks direct questions.”

“She does.”

“Does she always?”

“Usually.”

CC laughed.

Then she grew thoughtful.

“Do you think she wants to meet me because she’s curious?”

“Probably.”

“About me?”

“Yes.”

She tilted her head.

“Why?”

He gave her a smile.

“Because I’m serious about you.”

The answer was simple.

But it made her heart feel strangely full.

She looked down, her fingers playing with the edge of the blanket.

“I like that you told her.”

“I’m glad.”

“I don’t want to feel like a secret.”

Declan’s expression softened.

“You’re not.”

She looked up.

“I know you haven’t introduced me formally, and I understand why. We’re still taking our time.”

He nodded. “But I’m not hiding you. I simply want things to happen at a pace that feels right for both of us.”

She smiled.

“That’s what I want too.”

He looked at her.

“Good.”

His phone vibrated with a message from his mother, who was two rooms away.

Eleanor: Was CC comfortable?

He glanced at the screen, then smiled.

Declan: I think so.

Eleanor: She seemed very sweet.

Declan: She is.

Eleanor: I hope you know how lucky you are.

Declan read the message.

He didn’t reply immediately.

Then he typed:

Declan: I do.

A second message arrived.

Eleanor: And tell her she is welcome to visit whenever the time is right. No pressure.

Declan studied the screen.

Declan: I will.

He returned to the video call.

CC was looking at him.

“Your mother?”

He nodded.

“She asked whether you were comfortable.”

CC smiled.

“That’s very kind.”

“She also said you’re welcome to visit whenever the time is right.”

CC’s expression softened.

“Please thank her for me.”

“I will.”

She paused.

“Maybe one day.”

“Whenever you’re ready.”

She smiled.

The conversation eventually drifted towards Christmas traditions.

CC told him about how her family usually celebrated, how her parents would prepare food together, and how her mother always made too much.

Declan listened, asking questions about her childhood in Canada and the traditions she had kept after moving to Thailand.

“Do you miss celebrating with your parents?” he asked.

“Sometimes. Especially on days like this.”

She smiled.

“But we call. And they usually send me photographs of everything they’re eating.”

“Your mother sounds familiar.”

CC laughed.

“Maybe mothers are the same everywhere.”

“Perhaps.”

Declan held her gaze.

“Next year, I’d like to spend Christmas with you.”

She went still. “Here?”

“Here, or at the lake. Wherever you can get away to.”

“I’d like to see the tree.”

“Then I’ll make sure it’s there.”

She laughed. “Of course it will be.”

He smiled.

Then she looked at him more carefully.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then rest before dinner.”

“It’s three in the afternoon.”

“Rest anyway.”

He gave her an amused look.

“You’re becoming rather strict.”

“I’m learning from you.”

He laughed.

She smiled.

“Go. You have family dinner tonight and another family day tomorrow.”

“And you have rehearsal in the morning.”

“Then we’re both very busy people.”

She nodded.

Neither moved to end the call.

Declan studied her.

“CC?”

“Hmm?”

“I’m glad you met my mother.”

She smiled.

“Me too.”

“And I’m glad you liked her.”

“I did. She was lovely.”

He watched her.

Then he said, “Today would have been better with you in it.”

Her face softened.

“You were in mine.”

He leaned a little closer to the screen, as if the distance might somehow be reduced.

“Next time.”

She nodded.

“Next time.”

They exchanged goodnights, and CC waited until he ended the call.

The screen went dark.

She sat, looking at her reflection.

Then she smiled.

She had spoken to Eleanor Lincoln.

Not in a formal introduction, not at a family dinner, not as someone being presented for approval.

Just a brief hello on a Christmas video call.

And it had felt surprisingly easy.

Late that night, after the family dinner, Declan sat in his study with the photograph from the night before open on his phone: the tie, the study mirror, his own slightly self-conscious face.

His mother came in, holding a cup of tea.

“Still up?”

Declan looked up.

“Yes.”

“Was she happy, this afternoon?”

“She was.”

“Good.”

She placed the cup on the desk.

“I hope I didn’t make her nervous.”

Declan smiled.

“You were very kind.”

“I only said hello.”

“That’s enough.”

Eleanor looked at him.

Then her eyes moved to the tie, which he still hadn’t taken off.

“Twice in two days.”

“Father said the same.”

She smiled.

“It’s becoming one of your favourites.”

Declan looked down at the fabric.

“Perhaps.”

His mother gave him a knowing look.

“I’m glad.”

She turned to leave, then paused.

“Declan?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t make her feel that she has to wait for you to have time for her.”

He looked at his mother.

Eleanor’s expression was gentle.

“Your work will always be there. But people need to know they matter while they’re with you.”

Declan was quiet.

Then he nodded.

“She won’t.”

Eleanor smiled.

“Goodnight, darling.”

“Goodnight, Mother.”

After she left, Declan picked up his phone.

There were messages from CC, sent hours ago, while he was at dinner.

CC: I liked meeting your mother.

CC: I was nervous at first. But she’s very warm. I hope I can meet her properly one day.

CC: Merry Christmas again. Goodnight, Declan.

It was five in the morning in Bangkok. He typed anyway.

Declan: She liked meeting you too. She has already asked when she can hear you talk about your music.

Declan: Merry Christmas, my dear.

He placed the phone on the desk.

Outside, the winter night was quiet. The Christmas lights still glowed in the main hall, and somewhere downstairs, his parents were going to bed.

In Bangkok, CC would be asleep for another hour at least, with a wooden girl in a red coat standing guard on her coffee table.

The next step, he thought, didn’t need an announcement or a grand introduction. Just another dinner, another conversation, and one year, a chair waiting for her at the Christmas table.

chapters.title: Only You Get to Call Me That
chapters.desc: Back from Taipei, she finds flowers and an iced latte waiting in the car. In a quiet garden, he asks her properly to be his girlfriend, then asks if he may call her Cela.
chapters.epigraph: “Then Cela it is.”
chapters.content:
On a Friday in the middle of January, CC came home from four days of schedules in Taipei.

The fans were waiting in the arrival hall, as they always were. She waved, smiled, signed two albums without breaking stride, and let Nicha walk her out to the pick-up lane, where a dark car was waiting with its rear door already open.

The first thing she noticed when she got in was the flowers.

They weren’t extravagant. A bouquet of white ranunculus and pale pink tulips rested in the arms of the man in the back seat. He wore a charcoal coat over a dark sweater, one hand holding his phone, the other holding the flowers. His expression was composed, almost unreadable to anyone who didn’t know him.

But when he saw her, something in his face changed.

A quiet smile.

CC’s own appeared almost immediately.

The door closed behind her. Outside, the driver was already loading her suitcase.

“You’re early,” she said.

“By twelve minutes.”

“That’s early.”

“I didn’t want to risk being late.”

He looked at her, taking in her face, the tiredness around her eyes, the familiar little smile she was trying not to make too obvious.

Then he offered her the flowers.

“For you, sweetheart.”

She accepted them, looking down at the arrangement.

“They’re beautiful.”

“I thought you’d like them.”

“I do.”

In the cup holder beside her was an iced latte, half sweet, with the ice not yet melted. It was what she ordered when she thought no one was paying attention.

“How did you—”

“Nicha. I asked what you have after a flight.”

“She told you?”

“After some negotiation.”

She laughed.

He leaned over and kissed her cheek, a brief greeting that felt familiar now, behind tinted glass.

“Welcome back,” he murmured.

CC studied his face.

“So are you.”

“Then I’ll say it for both of us.”

She laughed again.

“That’s not how it works.”

“I’m willing to negotiate.”

The car pulled out into the airport traffic.

She had missed him.

Not in the dramatic way she sometimes imagined missing someone might feel. It was simpler than that. She had missed the ease of being beside him, the way he listened when she spoke, the quiet amusement in his eyes when she teased him, and the way he seemed to make even an ordinary afternoon feel like something worth remembering.

He had been in Munich for the New Year and had flown back to Bangkok that morning, and they had spoken every day. They had exchanged photographs, called whenever their schedules allowed, and occasionally fallen asleep on video calls with one of them still talking.

But a screen wasn’t the same as this.

A hand brushing hers.

His coat beside her shoulder.

The flowers she could actually hold.

“Are you hungry?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Would you like to eat first, or go home and rest?”

CC considered it.

“Home, I think.”

“Then home.”

Her eyes went to his.

“You don’t have to arrange everything around me.”

“I enjoy arranging things around you.”

He said it so naturally that she smiled.

He glanced at her.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s the second time you’ve said that today.”

“Maybe I have nothing to say.”

“I’m not convinced.”

She turned towards the window, smiling.

After a moment, she asked, “How was Munich?”

“Cold.”

“Very informative.”

He smiled.

“Quiet, mostly. My parents were pleased to have me home for a little longer.”

“Did your mother ask about me?”

“She did.”

CC turned back towards him.

“What did she ask?”

“Whether you were keeping well. Whether your schedule had become less demanding. And whether you liked tea. Before I could answer, she had packed some.”

CC laughed.

“She sent tea?”

“Through me.”

“Oh.”

“It’s in my luggage.”

She looked at him with mild disbelief.

“You brought tea all the way from Munich?”

“My mother asked me to.”

“And you agreed?”

“Of course.”

CC smiled, looking down at the flowers in her lap.

“That’s sweet.”

“She’s very pleased that you liked meeting her.”

“I liked meeting her too.”

“You told me. At five in the morning.”

“I mean it.”

He reached across the space between them and touched her fingers.

“She could tell.”

At her apartment, they had dinner delivered.

CC had changed into a soft cream cardigan and loose trousers, while Declan had taken off his coat and rolled the sleeves of his dark shirt to his forearms.

The flowers were arranged in a glass vase on the dining table.

They sat together, talking about the weeks they had spent apart. CC told him about a recording session that had gone longer than expected. Declan told her about a meeting with his father and a complicated acquisition that had occupied most of his attention.

She listened, occasionally asking questions.

He, in turn, remembered the smaller things she had mentioned in passing: a fitting she had disliked, a song she wanted to listen to again, a restaurant she had seen but hadn’t had time to visit.

At some point, CC rested her chin on her hand.

“You remember everything.”

“Not everything.”

“Almost everything I tell you.”

“I pay attention.”

She smiled. “You do.”

His eyes went to her face.

Then he said, “There’s something I’d like to ask you.”

Her face became attentive.

“What is it?”

“Not tonight.”

She blinked.

“Then why tell me?”

A faint smile touched his mouth.

“Because I wanted you to know I have something on my mind.”

“Is it serious?”

“Important.”

She studied his face.

He didn’t look worried. If anything, he seemed unusually thoughtful.

“Should I be nervous?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t be.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

She returned to her dinner, but she wondered what he had planned.

On Saturday afternoon, Declan took her somewhere.

He hadn’t explained much beyond that.

The car brought them to a private garden residence tucked away from the busier streets. It belonged to a family acquaintance and was occasionally used for small private gatherings. That afternoon, however, it was quiet.

The garden was shaded by old trees. A narrow stone path curved past a small pond, and white flowers grew along the edges. There was a covered terrace with a table prepared for two.

CC looked around.

“It’s lovely.”

“I thought you’d like somewhere quiet.”

She lifted her eyes to his.

“You’ve been planning this?”

“For a little while.”

“Since when?”

“Since Munich, perhaps.”

She smiled.

“That’s quite a long time.”

“I wanted to get it right.”

He offered her his hand.

She took it.

They walked through the garden before sitting down for tea. The afternoon passed gently. They talked about ordinary things: her upcoming schedule, his next trip to New York, the book she had started reading, and the possibility of taking a short holiday together when their calendars finally allowed it.

Declan didn’t rush the afternoon.

He let her finish her tea, asked whether she wanted another cup, and listened when she described a scene from the book with more enthusiasm than she had intended.

Eventually, the sunlight began to soften.

CC noticed that Declan had become quieter.

Not distant. Just thoughtful.

She set her cup down.

“Is this the important thing?”

He looked at her.

“Yes.”

She straightened slightly.

“Okay.”

He rested one hand on the table.

“CC, we’ve been seeing each other for some time now.”

She nodded.

“We have.”

“I’ve enjoyed every part of it. Even the distance, although I would prefer considerably less of that.”

She smiled.

“Me too.”

He continued, his voice calm.

“I told you when I came back to Bangkok that I wanted to court you seriously. Exclusively. I told you I wanted to take my time and do things properly.”

“I remember.”

“And I still mean everything I said.”

He paused, looking at her.

“But I’ve come to realise that I don’t want to keep calling this courtship simply because I haven’t asked you the question.”

CC’s expression softened.

She knew what he was about to say.

Still, she let him speak.

“I don’t want to assume that because we’ve kissed, because we’ve spent time together, or because we’ve been exclusive, you automatically want the next step.”

He leaned forward slightly.

“I want to ask you properly.”

Her fingers curled gently around the edge of her napkin.

Declan looked at her with the same steady attention he had given her from the beginning.

“CC, would you be my girlfriend?”

She didn’t answer. She wasn’t uncertain. The question meant more than she had expected it to. She looked at him, at the man who had once given her his shawl because she was cold, who remembered how she took her tea, who had crossed cities and time zones without making her feel indebted to him, who had made room for her in his life without asking her to rearrange hers around it.

She smiled.

“Yes.”

His face softened.

“Yes?”

She laughed a little.

“Yes, Declan. I’d love to.”

He held her gaze, as if he wanted to take in the answer properly.

Then he stood, walked around the table, and offered her his hand.

She placed hers in it.

He drew her gently to her feet.

“Come here.”

She stepped closer.

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Thank you,” he said.

CC considered him.

“For what?”

“For saying yes.”

She smiled.

“You don’t have to thank me.”

“I’m going to anyway.”

He bent and kissed her.

It wasn’t their first kiss. It was gentle and unhurried, the way the others had been.

But something had changed.

There was no longer a question waiting somewhere between them.

When he drew back, he was smiling.

“Hello, girlfriend.”

She laughed. “Hello, boyfriend.”

She laughed, then rested her forehead against his chest.

He wrapped his arms around her.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

They returned to their seats after a few minutes.

CC was still smiling.

Declan noticed.

“You seem pleased.”

“I am.”

“Good.”

She picked up her cup, then looked at him over the rim.

“So, what happens now?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Now?”

“Now that I’m your girlfriend.”

He considered the question with deliberate seriousness.

“I imagine I’ll continue taking you to dinner, sending you flowers, and trying to persuade you to let me carry your luggage.”

She laughed.

“That’s already happening.”

“Then I don’t anticipate a significant change in my behaviour.”

“That’s disappointing.”

He looked amused.

“Is it?”

She nodded, pretending to think.

“I thought there might be some benefits.”

“Such as?”

“I’m not sure. Perhaps more desserts.”

He smiled.

“That’s easily arranged.”

“And maybe you could be a little more affectionate.”

He gave her a quiet look.

“Is that a request?”

“Maybe.”

“Then I’ll consider it.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Declan.”

He laughed.

“Sweetheart, I think you’ll find I’m already rather affectionate.”

She smiled, unable to argue.

He reached across the table and took her hand.

“There is one thing I would like to change.”

“What?”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“I’d like to call you something.”

She tilted her head.

“What do you mean?”

“Your name.”

“CC?”

“Not that.”

She looked at him curiously.

He paused.

“Cela.”

Her face changed.

She knew the name, of course. It was her given name, the one on her passport, the one her parents used, especially when she was in trouble.

But Declan had always called her CC.

She glanced up at him.

“Cela?”

He nodded.

“Would you mind?”

She shook her head slowly.

“No. I wouldn’t.”

He watched her expression.

“It’s your name. I don’t want to use it if you prefer otherwise.”

She smiled.

“I like it.”

“Good.”

He said it once more.

“Cela.”

It wasn’t an unfamiliar name. It only sounded different in his voice, and unexpectedly intimate.

She lowered her eyes, smiling.

“Why do you want to call me that?”

“Because I like your name.”

She gave him a small, knowing look.

“That’s all?”

He smiled.

“Not quite.”

She waited.

“I’ve been calling you CC since we met. I like that name too. But Cela feels like something I’d like to keep for the moments when it’s just us.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“Just us?”

“Just us.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

Then she nodded.

“Okay.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Then Cela it is.”

She smiled.

“But only you. Not Nicha, not the company.”

His gaze returned to hers.

“And your parents?”

“My parents are allowed. They were first.”

“That seems fair.”

“Everyone else gets CC.”

He smiled, a little more warmly this time.

“I’d be honoured.”

On the drive back, the city was beginning to glow with evening lights.

CC sat beside Declan in the back seat, her hand resting in his. She had been quiet for several minutes, watching the passing buildings.

He glanced at her.

“What’s going through your mind?”

She turned towards him.

“I’m thinking about my name.”

“Your name?”

She nodded.

“You said it differently.”

He smiled.

“Did I?”

“Yes.”

“Would you like me to stop?”

She immediately shook her head.

“No.”

He gave her hand a gentle squeeze.

“Then I won’t.”

She smiled and looked out of the window again.

A few moments later, she said, “Can you say it again?”

He turned towards her.

“Cela?”

She nodded.

He said it.

“Cela.”

She smiled to herself.

Then he took out his phone, opened her contact, and changed CC ♡ to Cela. He turned the screen so she could see.

She looked at it. Then she took out her own phone. He had been Declan Lincoln, both names, like a business card, since Geneva.

She typed for a while and showed him: Declan (navy only).

“That’s slander,” he said.

“You can earn a new one.”

He watched her put her phone away, then leaned closer and kissed her temple.

“Happy, sweetheart?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

Back at her apartment, Declan stayed for dinner.

They ordered food, ate together, and spent the rest of the evening on her sofa. There was no grand celebration, no announcement, no photograph shared with the world.

CC didn’t feel the need to tell anyone immediately.

Neither did Declan.

The people closest to them might eventually know, but for now, the new word belonged to them.

Girlfriend.

Boyfriend.

A small change in language that somehow made everything feel more settled.

When Declan stood to leave, CC followed him to the door.

He put on his coat while she watched.

“Are you leaving already?”

He checked the time.

“It’s getting late.”

She pouted at him.

“It’s not that late.”

He smiled.

“Would you like me to stay longer?”

She hesitated, then nodded.

“A little.”

He considered her.

Then he took off his coat again and placed it over the back of the chair.

“Then I’ll stay a little longer.”

Her smile appeared immediately.

“Thank you.”

He walked towards her.

“Come here, Cela.”

She looked up at the name.

She stepped into his arms.

He held her close, one hand resting against the back of her head.

“Goodnight, sweetheart,” he murmured.

She smiled against his chest.

“Goodnight.”

He drew back just enough to look at her.

“Although I suppose I should say goodnight, girlfriend.”

She laughed.

“You sound very pleased with yourself.”

“I am.”

“Why?”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“Because I asked a question I’ve wanted to ask for some time, and received the answer I hoped for.”

She looked at him, smiling.

“Then I’m glad you asked.”

He kissed her forehead.

“So am I.”

At eighteen minutes to midnight, CC received a message.

Declan: Back at the hotel. The driver says congratulations.

CC: You told the driver?

Declan: I didn’t have to. Apparently I was humming.

She laughed into her pillow.

Then another message appeared.

Declan: Goodnight, Cela.

She read it twice.

Her smile softened.

CC: Goodnight, Declan.

She hesitated before typing again.

CC: I like being your girlfriend.

His reply came almost immediately.

Declan: I like having you as mine.

Then, a moment later:

Declan: And I rather like being your boyfriend.

She laughed, pressing her phone against her chest for a second before replying.

CC: I think I’ll keep you.

Declan: I was hoping you would.

She placed the phone on her bedside table.

The room was quiet, the flowers from the airport still resting on the dining table. Tomorrow, her schedule would resume. There would be rehearsals, meetings, and the usual demands of her work.

Declan would have his own responsibilities, his own meetings, his own flights to catch. Before any of that, there were five days in the Swiss mountains, starting next weekend, which he had booked while she was still saying yes to the girlfriend question, and which she had pretended to object to for almost a full minute.

Nothing about their lives had become simpler.

But something had become certain.

She was no longer wondering what they were.

And across the city, in a hotel suite above the river, a man who had spent years making decisions that affected thousands of people was smiling at a message from one woman.

He opened their conversation once more.

His thumb hovered over the screen.

Then he typed one final message.

Declan: Sleep well, Cela. I’ll call you tomorrow.

He looked at the name on the screen.

He would go on calling her sweetheart. But Cela wasn’t a name he intended to use in public, or let anyone borrow. Her parents had it first. He had it now, and no one else would.

chapters.title: A Little Life in the Mountains
chapters.desc: Five days on a farm above Grindelwald: goats, a first ski lesson in gloves he sent ahead, and two loaves of bread for two different cities.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s yours. That makes it fragile.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday morning, a week after she had said yes, CC was in Switzerland.

She had imagined their first holiday together would involve a beautiful hotel, perhaps a scenic restaurant, and a carefully planned itinerary.

She hadn’t expected to find herself standing in the middle of Zurich Airport, looking at a photograph of a cow.

A large, fluffy cow.

“Declan.”

He looked up from his phone.

“Yes, sweetheart?”

“Why is there a cow?”

He glanced at the screen she was holding out to him.

“Because we’re staying on a farm.”

She looked up.

“I know that. But why is there a cow in the photograph?”

“It’s part of the farm.”

She gave him a small, unimpressed look.

He smiled.

“Would you prefer I arrange for the cow to stay somewhere else?”

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

“I thought I’d ask.”

She laughed and put her phone away.

She had landed just after seven, on the overnight direct flight from Bangkok, in a seat he had booked that turned into a bed. Declan had come in from Munich an hour later. They had planned the holiday around a few days in the countryside, with skiing in the middle.

He had deliberately kept their schedule light.

CC had been working almost continuously over the previous months, and he had no intention of turning their first holiday into another itinerary she had to keep up with.

Their accommodation was a renovated alpine farmhouse above Grindelwald, in the Bernese Oberland, surrounded by snow-covered fields and mountain views. The property belonged to a family who had been farming the land for generations. A portion of the farmhouse had been converted into guest accommodation, retaining its wooden beams, stone fireplace, and traditional architecture.

It was comfortable, private, and far removed from the attention they usually received.

CC had liked the photographs immediately.

She had liked the idea of waking up somewhere quiet even more.

“Ready?” Declan asked.

She nodded.

He took her suitcase.

“I can carry it.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“I’m going to start charging you for saying that.”

“I’d be happy to pay.”

“Of course you would.”

He laughed and led her towards the waiting car.

The drive took a little over two hours, through small villages and winding mountain roads.

CC spent most of it looking out of the window.

The landscape gradually changed. Buildings became smaller, fields stretched farther, and snow settled more thickly along the roadside. Wooden houses stood beneath sloping roofs, their balconies decorated with flower boxes now covered in white.

At one point, she leaned closer to the window.

“Look.”

Declan glanced outside.

“What is it?”

“Those houses.”

He followed her gaze.

“They’re beautiful.”

“They look like something from a storybook.”

He smiled.

“Would you like to live in one?”

She considered it.

“Maybe for a week.”

“Only a week?”

“I would miss good restaurants.”

He laughed.

“I’ll remember that.”

When they finally arrived, a woman in her late fifties greeted them at the entrance.

“Welcome! You must be Declan and CC.”

Declan shook her hand.

“Thank you for having us.”

The woman introduced herself as Anna, the owner of the farm. She was warm and cheerful, with the sort of easy manner that made CC feel comfortable immediately.

“You must be tired after travelling,” Anna said. “Come inside. I’ll show you around.”

The farmhouse was even prettier than the photographs.

Dark wooden beams crossed the ceiling. A large stone fireplace occupied one side of the sitting room, and wide windows looked out over the snow-covered pasture. Their bedroom had a small balcony and a view of the mountains.

CC stood near the window.

“Oh.”

Declan came up behind her.

“Do you like it?”

She nodded.

“It’s lovely.”

He rested his hands lightly on her shoulders.

“I thought you’d enjoy the quiet.”

She turned her head slightly.

“I think I will.”

In the cupboard by the kettle, she found a tin of ginger tea, the same one that had turned up at a photo studio in Bangkok at seven in the morning. She held it up without a word. Declan looked out of the window.

Anna explained that breakfast would be served downstairs, and that guests were welcome to observe some of the farm’s daily activities if they wished.

CC immediately looked interested.

“Can we?”

Anna smiled.

“Of course. The animals are usually fed in the morning. You can come along if you’d like.”

CC nodded enthusiastically.

Declan glanced at her.

“Apparently, we have plans tomorrow morning.”

She smiled.

“We do.”

Declan woke to the feeling of someone moving beside him.

He opened his eyes.

CC was sitting up, looking towards the curtains.

“Good morning,” he murmured.

She turned.

“Good morning.”

“What’s the time?”

“Ten to seven.”

He glanced at the clock.

“That’s barely morning.”

“The cows have been up for hours.”

He studied her face.

“Why are you awake?”

She smiled.

“The animals.”

He laughed.

“You’re very enthusiastic about this.”

“You promised we’d go.”

“I did.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Come on.”

He looked at her.

Then he reached for her waist and gently pulled her back down.

“Five more minutes.”

She laughed.

“Declan.”

“I’m negotiating.”

“You’re delaying.”

“Five minutes is a reasonable compromise.”

She pushed out her lower lip.

He kissed her forehead.

“Come here, sweetheart.”

She settled against him, smiling.

Five minutes later, they were both getting dressed.

CC wore a cream wool sweater, dark trousers, and a padded jacket. Declan wore a charcoal knit sweater beneath a dark winter coat.

Anna met them near the barn.

“Good morning! You’re both early.”

“Good morning,” CC replied.

Anna showed them where to put their boots before leading them inside.

The barn was warm and smelled of hay. A few cows stood in their stalls, while others moved slowly in the adjoining area.

CC stopped beside one of them.

“Hello.”

The cow looked at her.

She looked at Declan.

“It’s looking at me.”

“I believe it is.”

“Do you think it likes me?”

Declan looked at the cow.

“I’m not qualified to interpret its feelings.”

Anna laughed.

“You can give her some hay.”

CC accepted the small bundle Anna offered.

She approached carefully, holding it out.

The cow leaned forward and began eating.

CC’s face brightened.

“Oh, she’s eating!”

Declan watched her, smiling.

“Yes, sweetheart. That’s generally what happens when you feed an animal.”

She turned towards him.

“You don’t have to comment on everything.”

“I wasn’t aware I was.”

Anna laughed again.

“You two are very sweet.”

CC looked down a little shy.

Declan, meanwhile, appeared perfectly comfortable.

After helping with the morning feeding, Anna showed them the smaller animals. CC spent a considerable amount of time with a pair of goats, one of which seemed determined to investigate the pockets of her jacket.

“She’s stealing from me,” CC announced.

Declan looked over.

“What has she taken?”

“I don’t know. But she’s looking.”

He approached and gently moved the goat away.

“Perhaps she thinks you have something interesting.”

CC watched him.

“Do you have anything interesting?”

“Not in my pockets.”

She smiled.

“That’s disappointing.”

They spent nearly an hour helping Anna before returning to the farmhouse for breakfast.

Declan had expected to enjoy the countryside.

He hadn’t expected to find himself taking photographs of CC feeding goats.

But he took several.

One showed her laughing as the goat nudged her jacket. Another captured her standing beside the cows, her cheeks pink from the cold.

He didn’t show her the photographs immediately.

He liked keeping little things for himself.

Breakfast was served in a small dining room overlooking the pasture.

There was fresh bread, butter, homemade jam, cheese, eggs, yoghurt, and fruit.

CC looked at the table.

“Everything looks so good.”

“Try the cheese,” Declan said.

She took a small piece.

“It’s from the farm?”

Anna nodded from the kitchen.

“Yes. We make some of it ourselves.”

CC tasted it and smiled.

“It’s delicious.”

Declan watched her take another piece.

“You like it?”

“Very much.”

“Would you like some more?”

She nodded.

He placed another portion on her plate.

She met his eyes.

“You’re spoiling me.”

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

He smiled.

“Then I’m doing rather well.”

She laughed and continued eating.

After breakfast, they spent the late morning walking around the property. The snow was soft beneath their boots, and the mountains looked almost impossibly close.

CC stopped to take photographs of the trees.

Declan stood beside her, hands in his coat pockets.

“Do you want me to take one of you?”

She turned.

“Together?”
