“If you’d like.”

She smiled and handed him her phone.

He took a few photographs, then returned it.

CC looked at them.

The first was a little too serious. The second showed her laughing.

The third caught Declan looking at her instead of the camera.

She paused.

“Declan.”

“Yes?”

“You weren’t looking at the camera.”

“I had a better view.”

She looked at the photograph again.

Then she smiled and saved it.

On the third morning, at First above Grindelwald, CC discovered two things about skiing.

The first was that it looked easier when other people did it.

The second was that Declan was much better at it than she had expected.

He stood beside her near the equipment area, fastening his gloves. Hers had been waiting at the farmhouse when they arrived, in a box with her name on it: pale grey, lined, exactly her size, with a slot for a small heat pad he had already put in.

She watched him.

“You’ve done this before.”

“A few times.”

“How many is a few?”

He looked at her.

“Enough.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

He smiled.

“I grew up coming to Switzerland occasionally. My parents liked skiing.”

“So you’re good?”

“Reasonably.”

She looked down at her own ski boots.

“I’m not.”

“I’d gathered.”

She looked up.

“How?”

“You’ve been studying the boots as though they’re a complicated piece of machinery.”

She laughed.

“They are complicated.”

He smiled and crouched slightly to check that her boots were fastened properly.

“Comfortable?”

“Mostly.”

“Anything hurting?”

“No.”

He stood.

“Good. We’ll take it slowly.”

They had arranged a private instructor for CC’s first proper lesson. Declan had offered to teach her himself, but she had declined.

“I don’t want you to spend the entire morning worrying about me falling.”

He had looked amused.

“I wouldn’t mind.”

“I would.”

So they had agreed on an instructor.

For the first hour, CC concentrated on learning how to stand, move, and stop. She was careful, a little tense, and occasionally frustrated when her skis seemed to have a mind of their own.

Declan watched from a short distance away.

He didn’t interfere.

When she finally managed to make it down a gentle slope without falling, he applauded.

CC looked towards him, smiling broadly.

“Did you see?”

“I did.”

“I didn’t fall!”

“An excellent achievement.”

She laughed.

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m not surprised, sweetheart. I’m impressed.”

She smiled and continued towards him.

Then, as she reached the bottom, one ski slipped slightly.

Declan stepped forward instinctively.

She caught herself, but her face changed.

He was beside her immediately.

“Are you all right?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Sure?”

“Yes. Just surprised.”

He checked her balance before letting her move again.

“Take your time.”

She turned to him.

“I’m trying.”

“You’re doing well.”

His voice was calm, without a trace of impatience.

She smiled.

“Will you stay with me?”

“Of course.”

And he did.

For the rest of the morning, he stayed nearby, occasionally offering encouragement, never making her feel slow or inexperienced.

By lunchtime, CC had improved.

She was still cautious, but she had begun to enjoy herself.

They stopped at a mountain restaurant overlooking the slopes.

CC sat down with a satisfied sigh.

“My legs are tired.”

Declan removed his gloves.

“Understandable.”

She held his gaze.

“Are you tired?”

“Not particularly.”

“Of course not.”

He smiled.

“Would you like something warm?”

“Hot chocolate.”

“Anything to eat?”

She read the menu.

“Maybe soup.”

He ordered for both of them, making sure they had a table near the window.

When their drinks arrived, CC wrapped both hands around her cup.

She took a sip.

Then she looked at him.

“This is a very good holiday.”

He smiled.

“I’m glad.”

“I like the farm.”

“I noticed.”

“And the skiing.”

“Even after this morning?”

She laughed.

“Yes. Especially after I managed not to fall.”

He raised his cup.

“To your successful morning.”

She clinked hers gently against his.

“To not falling.”

By the time they returned to the farmhouse, CC was exhausted.

She had changed into soft clothes and was sitting on the rug in front of the fireplace, her legs stretched out beneath a blanket.

Declan came downstairs with two cups of tea.

He placed one on the low table beside her.

“Here.”

She looked up.

“Thank you.”

He sat on the sofa behind her.

“How are your legs?”

“Still attached.”

He laughed.

“That’s reassuring.”

She leaned back against the sofa, resting her head near his knee.

“I’m tired.”

“I can see that.”

“Will you massage my legs?”

He looked down at her.

“Of course.”

She smiled and shifted slightly so he could sit more comfortably.

He moved closer and gently began massaging her calves through the soft fabric of her trousers.

CC closed her eyes.

For several minutes, the room was quiet except for the crackling fireplace.

Then she said, “I think I want to do this again tomorrow.”

“Skiing?”

She nodded.

“Maybe I’ll be better.”

“I suspect you will.”

She opened one eye.

“Will you ski with me?”

“Of course.”

“Not go ahead?”

He looked amused.

“I’ll stay with you.”

She smiled and closed her eyes again.

After a while, she reached for his hand.

He stopped and let her take it.

She turned his palm upward and traced the lines lightly with her finger.

“Thank you for bringing me here.”

He looked down at her.

“You don’t have to thank me.”

“I want to.”

He brushed her hair away from her cheek.

“I wanted to spend time with you somewhere we could both forget about work for a little while.”

She smiled.

“I think we have.”

He kissed her forehead.

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“Do you like it?”

“The farm?”

“The holiday.”

He considered the question.

“I like waking up with you. I like having breakfast with you. I like watching you make friends with animals that seem determined to steal your clothes.”

She laughed.

“And?”

“I like that you ask me to ski with you even though I’m not very good at being patient on beginner slopes.”

She gave him a look.

“You’ve been very patient.”

“Then I’m improving.”

She smiled.

He dipped his head and kissed her gently.

When he drew back, she was still smiling.

“I’m glad it’s you,” she whispered.

His face softened.

“So am I, Cela.”

On the fourth morning, CC had decided she wanted to help Anna prepare breakfast.

Declan discovered this when he came downstairs and found her standing in the kitchen wearing an apron.

He stopped at the doorway.

“What are you doing?”

She turned.

“Helping.”

He looked at the apron.

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

Anna laughed from beside the counter.

“She is. She’s been helping me with the bread.”

Declan approached.

“Should I be concerned?”

CC tilted her head.

“Why?”

“I’ve never seen you look so serious about flour.”

She gave him her best wounded look.

“I’m concentrating.”

He smiled and kissed her cheek.

“Then I won’t disturb you.”

But he stayed.

He watched her knead the dough, occasionally brushing flour from the counter. When she asked him to hold a bowl, he did. When Anna asked him to fetch something from the pantry, he went without complaint.

At one point, CC noticed a little flour on his sleeve.

She reached over and brushed it away.

“There.”

He looked over.

“Thank you.”

“You’re helping.”

“I’m doing my best.”

She smiled. “It shows.”

Anna watched them with a fond expression.

“You make a good team.”

Declan glanced at CC.

“I think so.”

CC lowered her eyes, smiling.

Later, when they sat down to breakfast, Anna placed two small loaves in front of them.

“One each. You’re going to different cities, Declan tells me.”

CC looked delighted.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“Thank you so much.”

Declan looked at the loaf.

“We’ll have to make room in the luggage.”

She smiled. “Mine is coming home with me.”

“Then we’ll make room.”

Their final morning arrived too quickly.

CC stood on the balcony in a thick sweater, looking out over the fields.

The sky was pale, and the mountains were quiet beneath their covering of snow.

Declan came out carrying two cups of coffee.

He handed one to her.

“Good morning.”

She accepted it.

“Good morning.”

He stood beside her.

“Enjoying the view?”

She nodded.

“I don’t want to leave.”

He smiled.

“We can come back.”

“Promise?”

“Of course.”

She turned towards him.

“Next time, I want to spend more time with the animals.”

“Not more skiing?”

“Both.”

“Then we’ll arrange it.”

She smiled and leaned against his shoulder.

They stood there, drinking their coffee.

After a while, she said, “I think I understand why you wanted somewhere like this.”

He looked down at her.

“Why?”

“Because nobody expects anything from us here.”

He listened.

“We can wake up, eat breakfast, walk around, do silly things. Nobody is waiting for me to perform or for you to attend a meeting.”

He smiled.

“Exactly.”

She looked towards the fields.

“I like being ordinary with you.”

Declan turned slightly towards her.

“Sweetheart.”

She looked up.

“I don’t think there’s anything ordinary about having you here.”

She laughed.

“You know what I mean.”

“I do.”

He took her free hand.

“And I like it too.”

She rested her head against his shoulder.

“Can we have more holidays like this?”

“As many as you’d like.”

She smiled.

“Don’t promise too much.”

He kissed the top of her head.

“I’m quite comfortable with that promise.”

That afternoon, they were back at Zurich Airport. Her flight to Bangkok left first, and his to Munich an hour after it.

They stood together near the departure area. Zurich wasn’t Bangkok; no one here was looking for her.

CC had her coat over one arm and her handbag on her shoulder.

Declan held the small bag with her loaf from the farmhouse.

She looked at it.

“You’re carrying the bread.”

“Yes.”

“It’s not fragile.”

“It’s yours. That makes it fragile.”

She laughed.

He reached for her hand.

“Did you enjoy your first holiday with me?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

“Good.”

“I liked the farm. I liked skiing. I liked breakfast.”

“And the goats?”

She smiled.

“Especially the goats.”

He laughed.

“I’ll remember that.”

She looked at him.

“Thank you for making it so lovely.”

He brushed his thumb over her hand.

“You made it lovely.”

She smiled.

Then he bent and kissed her.

It was a familiar goodbye, but somehow a little different now. They were no longer wondering what they meant to each other. They had a place in each other’s lives, and this holiday had given them something that belonged entirely to them.

When they drew apart, CC looked at him.

“Next time, somewhere with a beach?”

He smiled.

“Certainly.”

“And no goats.”

“I can’t guarantee that.”

She laughed.

“Declan!”

He kissed her forehead.

“Go on, sweetheart. You’ll be late.”

She stepped away, then turned back.

“Call me when you land.”

“I will.”

“And send me the goat photos. All of them.”

He smiled.

“Yes, Cela.”

She grinned.

Then she took her bread from him and walked towards security.

Declan watched her until she disappeared into the crowd.

A few minutes later, his phone vibrated.

Cela: I already miss the farm.

He smiled.

Declan: We haven’t even left Switzerland.

Cela: I’m at the gate. That counts.

Declan: I’ll take you back.

Cela: Promise?

Declan: Promise.

A photograph followed.

It was the picture he had taken on the first morning at the farm: CC standing beside the cow, laughing, her hair slightly windswept and her cheeks pink from the cold.

Declan: I think she misses you too.

CC replied almost immediately.

Cela: Tell her I’ll come back.

He took in the photograph again, smiling to himself.

Then he typed:

Declan: I’ll tell her, sweetheart.

He put his phone away and picked up his own loaf of bread.

Their first holiday was over, and he already knew which photograph he would keep. Not the mountains or the farmhouse. CC laughing beside a cow, her cheeks pink from the cold. Nothing about it was extraordinary, and it was the best thing on his phone.

chapters.title: The Most Entertaining Thing on His Screen
chapters.desc: Her variety show comes out, and Declan watches a thirty-one-second dance more times than he will admit. Frankfurt waits half an hour.
chapters.epigraph: “A very strange potato, sweetheart.”
chapters.content:
On Thursday afternoon, the day after they left Switzerland, Declan had a video conference scheduled for three.

He had finished reviewing the documents Alexander had sent him, answered two messages from his father, and was now sitting in his office with a glass of water beside his laptop. In Bangkok, it was half past eight in the evening.

His phone lit up.

Cela: Are you working?

He glanced at the message and smiled.

Declan: I was. I’m taking a break.

Cela: Good.

Declan: How was your day, sweetheart?

Cela: Busy. I landed this morning and went straight to filming.

Declan: Straight from the plane?

Cela: I slept on the plane. In the bed you booked.

Declan: Everything went well?

Cela: Yes! I think it was fun.

Declan: What did you film?

Cela: A variety show. I’ll send you the link when it’s released.

Declan: I’ll look forward to it.

Cela: Don’t expect too much. I was just talking most of the time.

Declan smiled at that.

Declan: I can’t imagine that being a problem.

Cela: Declan.

Declan: What?

Cela: You’re biased.

Declan: Undoubtedly.

She sent him a laughing emoji.

He put the phone down and returned to his work.

He didn’t think much more about the programme until the following Wednesday afternoon, when CC sent him a message with a link.

Cela: It’s out!

A second message followed.

Cela: Please don’t laugh at me.

Declan checked the screen.

Then he smiled.

Declan: Now I’m particularly interested.

Cela: That’s not reassuring.

Declan: I’ll be kind.

Cela: You’d better.

It was twenty to four. Frankfurt was at a quarter past. He opened the link.

The programme began with a lively introduction.

It was a popular Korean-style entertainment format adapted for Thai television, with a panel of hosts, rotating celebrity guests, games, conversations, and a few unexpected challenges.

CC appeared a little after the opening segment.

She was wearing a soft blue outfit, her hair falling neatly over her shoulders. Her makeup was light, and she smiled politely as the hosts welcomed her.

Declan leaned back.

He had seen her in countless photographs. He had attended events where she was surrounded by cameras, watched her perform under stage lights, and seen the polished version of her that the public knew.

But he still found himself looking at her as if he hadn’t seen her in a while.

She was beautiful.

He knew that already.

It wasn’t a new discovery.

Yet sometimes, when he saw her unexpectedly, the thought arrived with such force that he had to pause.

Her face was delicate without looking fragile. Her expressions were lovely because she never seemed to realise how much they changed. When she listened, her eyes were attentive. When she was amused, her smile appeared gradually, almost as if she were trying to contain it.

And when she laughed—

Declan’s mouth curved.

He had always thought her laughter was one of his favourite things.

On screen, one of the hosts asked her about her hobbies.

CC answered politely.

“I like reading, listening to music, and sometimes cooking.”

The host asked what she liked to cook.

“Usually simple things. Soup, noodles, congee.”

“Can you cook well?”

CC considered the question.

“I think I can cook enough to feed myself.”

The hosts laughed.

She smiled, then added, “I’m not sure whether that’s the same as cooking well.”

Declan laughed.

He paused the video, looking at her frozen expression.

Then he shook his head, smiling to himself.

“Sweetheart.”

He resumed.

The host asked whether she ever cooked for other people.

“Sometimes.”

“Do people enjoy it?”

“I think so. Nobody has complained.”

The panel laughed again.

One of the hosts leaned forward.

“Maybe they’re afraid of you.”

CC’s eyes widened.

“Why would they be afraid?”

“Because you’re beautiful. Maybe they’re too nervous to tell you the truth.”

She looked genuinely puzzled.

Then she said, seriously, “But if the food is bad, I should know. Otherwise, I’ll keep making it.”

Declan laughed.

Not a polite laugh.

A proper one.

He leaned back, his eyes still on the screen.

She hadn’t done anything extraordinary. She wasn’t trying to be funny. She wasn’t performing a rehearsed joke or deliberately creating a moment for the camera.

She was answering questions.

And somehow, that was enough.

The programme moved into a game segment.

The guests were asked to identify objects from close-up photographs. CC was given a picture of something that looked like a complicated kitchen utensil.

She stared at it for several seconds.

“Is it a potato?”

The host blinked.

“A potato?”

“Maybe a very strange potato.”

The panel burst into laughter.

The photograph was revealed to be a kitchen scrubber.

CC looked at it.

“Oh.”

She nodded, accepting the result.

“I was close.”

The host laughed.

“How was that close?”

“They’re both in the kitchen.”

Declan covered his mouth.

He glanced at the screen, then at the time. He had a meeting in less than twenty minutes.

He should stop watching.

Instead, he adjusted his position and continued.

The next segment involved the guests answering questions about their habits.

One host asked CC what she usually did when she was nervous.

She thought about it.

“I become quiet.”

“Really? You don’t look nervous.”

“I think that’s because I become even quieter.”

The host laughed.

“Then how do we know you’re nervous?”

CC smiled.

“You probably don’t.”

Declan’s expression softened.

He liked that answer.

It was so distinctly her: honest, unembellished, and funny without trying to be.

He watched her listen to the other guests, nodding when they spoke, occasionally adding a small comment that made the hosts laugh.

She was comfortable.

Not overly talkative, not trying to dominate the conversation, but attentive and naturally responsive.

He enjoyed the programme far more than he had anticipated.

At one point, she laughed at something another guest said and leaned forward, covering her mouth.

Declan paused the video.

He stared at the screen.

Her eyes were almost closed from laughing.

He smiled.

Then, he said, “You’re ridiculous.”

He resumed the programme.

The show moved into a short challenge.

The hosts announced that each guest would have to demonstrate a popular TikTok dance.

CC looked immediately uncomfortable.

Declan straightened.

The host turned towards her.

“CC, do you know this dance?”

She studied the screen they were showing her.

“I’m not sure.”

The host laughed.

“You’re an idol. Surely you know TikTok dances.”

CC gave a small, helpless smile.

“I’m an idol, but I’m not necessarily good at TikTok dances.”

Declan’s eyebrows lifted.

He was already smiling.

The hosts explained the choreography.

It was a short dance, cheerful and slightly playful, with a sequence of hand movements, a small shoulder movement, and a final pose.

CC watched carefully.

Then she tried it once.

She missed one of the movements.

The hosts laughed.

She stopped and looked at them.

“Wait. I need to see it again.”

The host replayed the demonstration.

CC nodded with concentration.

“Okay. I understand.”

She tried again.

This time, she got most of it right, but her timing was slightly off.

She looked towards the host.

“Was that correct?”

“Almost!”

She smiled.

“Almost is good.”

Declan laughed.

Then the music started again.

CC stood in front of the camera.

And did the dance.

She wasn’t trying to make it look cute. She followed the choreography, her expression focused at first, then gradually turning into a smile when she reached the final movement.

At the end, she tilted her head slightly and made the final pose.

The hosts applauded.

One of them exclaimed, “That’s so cute!”

CC laughed, looking a little embarrassed.

“Thank you.”

Declan didn’t move.

He stared at the screen.

The programme continued, but he was still thinking about the dance.

He rewound.

Watched it again.

Then once more.

He sat back, smiling in disbelief.

“Oh, sweetheart.”

He replayed it.

The little movement of her shoulders. The way she had looked so concentrated at the beginning. The smile that appeared when she realised she had managed to get through it.

The final pose.

He watched it again.

Then he laughed, shaking his head.

It was absurd.

He had seen her perform complicated choreography on enormous stages. He had watched her dance in music videos with professional lighting, elaborate costumes, and perfectly coordinated movements.

But somehow, this thirty-second segment was proving more difficult to stop watching.

He replayed it again.

His phone rang.

Alexander.

Declan glanced at the time.

“Alexander.”

“Mr. Lincoln, I wanted to confirm whether we’re proceeding with Frankfurt at a quarter past four.”

Declan looked at the laptop.

The programme was paused on CC’s final pose.

“Yes. Give me five minutes.”

“Certainly.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Everything all right?”

Declan glanced at the screen again.

“Quite.”

“Very good. I’ll have everyone ready.”

The call ended.

Declan looked at the video.

Then he pressed play again.

Five minutes later, Alexander received another message.

Declan: Move Frankfurt to a quarter to five, please.

Alexander reread the message.

He glanced at the calendar.

Then he replied.

Alexander: Certainly, Mr. Lincoln.

He didn’t ask why.

He had worked for Declan long enough to recognise when a matter wasn’t urgent enough to interrupt his employer’s attention.

And lately, there seemed to be a specific person capable of doing that.

Declan finally reached for his phone.

Declan: I’ve watched your programme.

CC replied a few seconds later.

Cela: Already?

Declan: Yes.

Cela: Was it okay?

He smiled.

Declan: Very entertaining.

Cela: Really?

Declan: You were very good.

Cela: I didn’t do much.

Declan: That was precisely the point.

She sent a confused emoji.

Cela: What does that mean?

Declan: You made an entire programme enjoyable simply by being yourself.

There was a pause.

Then:

Cela: You’re being biased again.

Declan: I warned you I was.

She sent a laughing emoji.

Then another message.

Cela: Did you see the dance?

Declan checked the screen.

He smiled.

Declan: I did.

Cela: I was so embarrassed.

Declan: Why?

Cela: Because I didn’t know the dance properly.

Declan: You did perfectly well.

Cela: I almost missed the last part.

Declan: I noticed.

She sent a horrified emoji.

Cela: You noticed?!

He laughed.

Declan: I noticed everything.

Cela: That’s embarrassing.

Declan: I thought it was adorable.

A moment passed.

Then she replied.

Cela: Please don’t replay it.

Declan glanced at the screen.

He glanced at the video still open on his laptop.

Then he typed.

Declan: I wasn’t planning to.

He paused.

Then added:

Declan: Although I may have watched it a few times.

CC’s reply came almost immediately.

Cela: DECLAN.

He laughed.

Declan: What?

Cela: How many times?

He considered lying.

Then decided against it.

Declan: Enough to know the choreography.

She sent a series of embarrassed emojis.

He smiled so broadly that he had to put his phone down.

At twenty-four minutes past four, CC called him. In Bangkok, it was nearly half past ten.

He answered almost immediately.

Her face appeared on the screen. She was sitting on her sofa, wearing a soft white top, her hair loosely tied back.

She looked at him with narrowed eyes.

“Why did you watch it so many times?”

He settled back.

“Because I liked it.”

“It’s only a short dance.”

“Thirty-one seconds.”

“You’ve seen me dance properly.”

“I have.”

“Then why?”

He smiled.

“Would you like an honest answer?”

She nodded.

“Because you looked very cute.”

Her face changed.

“Declan.”

He laughed.

“What?”

“You’re making it sound like I was doing something ridiculous.”

“You weren’t.”

“Then why are you laughing?”

“Because I find you very endearing.”

She looked away, smiling despite herself.

He watched her.

There was something about her expression that made him want to reach through the screen and pull her into his arms.

It wasn’t that he found her beautiful.

He did, very much.

But there were moments when her beauty seemed to make him almost helplessly fond of her.

The way she blinked when she was confused. The way she tried to hide her smile.

The way she became slightly defensive when she was embarrassed, even though she was clearly pleased.

He had a strange urge to kiss her forehead, pinch her cheeks gently, and tell her she was too lovely for her own good.

It was an almost overwhelming tenderness, bordering on ridiculous.

He had once heard someone call it cuteness aggression.

He understood the phrase better now.

“What’s that expression?” CC asked.

He watched her.

“What expression?”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to?”

“You’re smiling like you know something.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“I do know something.”

“What?”

“That I miss you.”

Her face softened.

“Oh.”

“And that I would very much like to kiss you right now.”

She smiled.

“You could have said that earlier.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Would you have allowed it?”

She nodded.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

She gave him a small, playful look.

“You’ll have to come and find out.”

He laughed.

“That’s a rather tempting invitation.”

She smiled, then rested her chin on her hand.

“Did you really watch the whole programme?”

“From beginning to end.”

“Even the game?”

“Yes.”

“Even when I got the answer wrong?”

“Especially then.”

She looked offended.

“Why?”

“Because you looked so certain that a kitchen scrubber was a potato.”

She burst out laughing.

“It looked like one!”

He laughed with her.

“A very strange potato, sweetheart.”

She covered her face.

“I can’t believe you watched that.”

“I enjoyed every minute.”

She lowered her hands.

“Even the dance?”

He tilted his head.

“Especially the dance.”

She groaned.

“Please.”

He smiled.

“I’m afraid that part may become a favourite.”

She gave him a look.

“Don’t you dare show anyone.”

“I wouldn’t.”

His answer was immediate and sincere.

He wouldn’t share something because he found it adorable. The moment belonged to her, and he liked being the person who could enjoy it privately.

CC seemed to understand.

She smiled.

“Good.”

The conversation continued for another twenty minutes, while Frankfurt waited without knowing it.

CC told him about the filming day, the hosts, and how one of them had insisted she try the dance again after the first attempt.

Declan listened, occasionally asking questions.

Then she remembered something.

“Oh, I forgot.”

“What?”

“The producer said the clip might be posted separately.”

He looked interested.

“Will it?”

“I think so.”

“Then I’ll look forward to it.”

She smiled.

“You’ve already seen it.”

“I can watch it again.”

She laughed.

“Of course you can.”

He glanced at the time.

“Shouldn’t you be getting ready for bed?”

“Are you telling me to sleep?”

“I’m suggesting it.”

“Because you have work?”

“Because I want you to rest.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

He looked at her.

“Goodnight, Cela.”

Her face softened at the name.

“Goodnight, Declan.”

“Sleep well, sweetheart.”

“You too.”

They ended the call.

Declan returned to the programme.

He watched the final segment, then closed the page.

His meeting with Frankfurt began shortly afterwards.

The meeting ended a little before six.

Alexander sent him the revised documents for the following morning, and Declan reviewed the first few pages before closing his laptop.

His phone lit up with a notification.

CC had sent him a short video.

It was the TikTok dance clip, edited into a vertical format.

Cela: They posted it.

He opened it.

Watched once.

Then again.

The third time, he caught himself smiling at the same moment she had smiled during the final pose.

He shook his head.

There was no reasonable explanation for how much he enjoyed such a small thing.

He typed:

Declan: I’ve seen it.

Cela: And?

Declan: Still adorable.

Cela: You need a hobby.

Declan: I appear to have found one.

Cela: Unfortunately.

He laughed.

Declan: Very unfortunate.

She sent him a heart.

Declan saved the video.

Not to a public folder, not to anything shared with his assistants.

Just to his own phone.

He gave it a private name.

Cela — TikTok.

That night, at home, he placed the phone on his bedside table and turned off the light.

A few minutes later, he picked it up again.

He watched the video one last time.

Or at least, he told himself it would be the last time.

On Thursday morning, Alexander entered Declan’s office with a folder.

“Good morning, Mr. Lincoln.”

“Good morning.”

Alexander placed the folder on his desk.

“The Frankfurt team has confirmed the revised figures. I’ve also moved your afternoon call to accommodate the New York office.”

“Thank you.”

Alexander noticed the phone beside the folder.

The screen was illuminated.

A familiar young woman was frozen mid-dance.

He looked at it for half a second.

Then looked away.

Declan followed his gaze.

A faint smile appeared.

“Something to add, Alexander?”

“No, sir.”

“Good.”

Alexander opened his notebook.

“Your first meeting is at nine.”

“I’m aware.”

There was a brief pause.

Then Alexander, with the careful neutrality of a man who valued his employment, said, “I hope you enjoyed the programme.”

Declan looked up.

He said nothing.

Then he smiled.

“Very much.”

Alexander nodded.

“I’m glad to hear it.”

He turned to leave.

“Alexander.”

“Yes, sir?”

“Send me the link to the full episode. I’d like to keep it.”

Alexander paused.

“Of course.”

When he left, Declan picked up his phone.

He opened the saved clip again.

His girlfriend appeared on screen, smiling at the camera, looking slightly embarrassed and entirely unaware of how much affection she was about to inspire.

Declan watched her move through the little choreography.

Then he smiled to himself.

He had spent years surrounded by people who were impressive.

People who could command a room, negotiate a deal, deliver a performance, or hold the attention of thousands.

CC could do all of those things.

But what he loved most was that she didn’t need to do any of them to make him happy.

Sometimes she only had to answer a question about a potato.

He watched the dance once more before his first meeting.

chapters.title: The View from the Other Side
chapters.desc: He tells her he’s tied up with meetings that weekend, then watches BLUE HOUR from a suite at Impact Arena. Backstage, Nicha has emptied a room.
chapters.epigraph: “You hold the microphone with both hands for the first song.”
chapters.content:
Declan had attended concerts before.

He had sat through private performances at charity galas, listened to orchestras in halls with ceilings painted by artists long dead, and watched internationally acclaimed musicians perform from seats that cost more than most people’s annual salaries. He understood the mechanics of a large production. The lighting, the sound engineering, the choreography, the logistics of moving hundreds of people through a venue without anyone noticing the machinery behind it.

He had never enjoyed the noise.

Tonight, at Impact Arena on the first Saturday of February, he was beginning to suspect that he had misunderstood something.

“Mr. Lincoln, the performance will begin in approximately fifteen minutes.”

Declan glanced at his watch.

“Thank you, Alexander.”

His assistant stood beside him in the private viewing suite, holding a tablet. Through the glass, the enormous concert hall was gradually filling. Thousands of people were finding their seats, waving light sticks, taking photographs of the stage, and calling out the names of the performers.

BLUE HOUR filled the screens: four girls who had debuted together at nineteen and had been filling arenas ever since. On the banners in the crowd, one name appeared more than any other.

CC.

Declan looked at it.

Then his phone vibrated.

Cela: Are you still working?

He smiled.

Declan: For the moment.

Cela: Don’t work too late.

Declan: I’ll try to behave.

A few seconds passed.

Cela: That doesn’t sound convincing.

He leaned back in his seat.

Declan: I’m capable of behaving when properly motivated.

Cela: You sound very confident.

Declan: I have a good incentive.

He could almost picture her expression.

She was probably sitting in front of a mirror while someone adjusted her hair, reading his message with that small, reluctant smile she tried not to show when other people were around.

He put the phone away.

Alexander looked at him.

“Would you like me to have the refreshments brought in?”

“No, thank you.”

“Of course.”

Alexander hesitated before adding, “P’Nicha will bring you through the staff corridor after the performance. Miss Chanya has not been told, as you asked.”

“Good.”

“The suite is booked under Lincoln Group, as a brand partner. No one will think twice.”

“Thank you, Alexander.”

Alexander’s expression remained perfectly professional.

Declan looked back towards the stage.

He had told CC that he might be occupied with business this weekend. Technically, he hadn’t lied. He had meetings in Bangkok, two dinners with regional partners, and a Monday morning departure. He had neglected to mention that he had arranged his schedule around her concert.

He wanted to see her perform.

Not through a screen, not through a carefully edited recording, and not through the occasional video she sent him from rehearsals.

He wanted to see her from the audience.

To understand, even, what it felt like to be one of the thousands of people who looked towards the stage and waited for her to appear.

The lights went down.

The crowd erupted.

And Declan finally understood that he had underestimated the volume of affection a person could receive from strangers.

The opening performance began with a burst of light. The group appeared onstage in coordinated outfits, moving through the first sequence with the precision of people who had rehearsed the same eight counts until their bodies could remember them without thought.

The audience screamed.

Declan watched.

He recognised CC immediately.

Her hair was styled differently from how she usually wore it, and the stage makeup sharpened her features. Under the lights, she looked almost unfamiliar.

Then she smiled.

It wasn’t the polite smile she gave interviewers, or the smaller one she saved for his teasing. It was brighter, confident, and entirely at ease.

She moved with the music, her expressions changing naturally as the performance unfolded. She knew where the cameras were. She knew when to turn, when to hold a pose, when to let the audience see her.

She was good.

He had known she was good.

But watching her from this distance made him appreciate something different: how much of herself she gave to the people in front of her.

When her part came, the audience sang along.

Declan watched the people rather than the stage.

A young girl in the front section was holding a banner with CC’s name written in silver letters. Two friends beside her were jumping excitedly. Further back, a group of fans held up photographs from different eras of the group.

They were happy.

Because of her.

He returned his attention to the stage.

A small smile appeared on his face.

The first unexpected moment happened halfway through the concert. The group had just finished a song when the lighting changed for the next segment. A brief technical delay followed.

The members stood together near the centre of the stage while the crew worked behind the screens.

One of the other members leaned towards CC and whispered something.

CC looked at her, then at the audience.

She laughed.

The crowd immediately reacted.

A microphone was brought to her.

“Sorry,” she said in Thai, smiling. “They’re making us wait a little.”

The audience cheered.

She glanced towards the side of the stage, where the crew were still working, then turned back.

“Should we talk while they fix it?”

The crowd screamed louder.

She listened to someone calling her name.

“CC!”

“Yes?”

“Are you hungry?”

She blinked.

Then she laughed, genuinely caught off guard.

“That’s a very important question.”

The audience laughed with her.

“Have you eaten?” another person shouted.

CC looked towards the audience, her expression turning thoughtful.

“I had something before coming here.”

A pause.

“But I’m thinking about what to eat after.”

The crowd erupted again.

Declan’s smile deepened.

One of the members leaned into her microphone.

“She has been thinking about food all day.”

CC turned towards her with an expression of mild betrayal.

“That’s not true.”

The member nodded solemnly.

“She asked what we were having after rehearsal.”

“That was a reasonable question.”

The audience laughed.

CC shook her head, looking down before lifting her microphone again.

“I’m just making sure everyone eats properly.”

She wasn’t trying to be funny. She was responding as herself, with a quiet sincerity that made even the smallest remark entertaining.

Declan looked down, smiling to himself, and sent Nicha one message: What does she eat after a show?

The lights came back on.

The members cheered, and the audience followed.

CC turned towards the stage crew and gave them a small thumbs-up.

The concert continued.

By the time the final song began, Declan had stopped checking his phone entirely.

He had missed two messages from Alexander and one from a business partner.

He didn’t care.

The stage was now bathed in warm golden light. The group stood in a line, their voices blending with the music as the final chorus approached.

CC stood slightly to the left.

Her face softened as she looked out over the crowd.

There was a moment when she seemed to recognise someone holding a particular banner. She pointed towards them, smiled, and waved.

The fan nearly collapsed.

Declan watched the exchange.

He understood, watching it, that the person he knew privately belonged to a much larger world.

There were people who had followed her for years, people who had found comfort in her music, people who knew the smallest details of her career and had travelled across cities to see her tonight.

He wasn’t threatened by it.

Nor did he feel any need to claim a part of her that belonged to someone else.

He felt proud.

When the final notes ended, the audience rose to their feet.

CC bowed with the others.

“Thank you for coming tonight,” she said in Thai. “Please get home safely. And don’t forget to eat something.”

The audience laughed.

She smiled.

Then she added, more, “Thank you for staying with us.”

Declan applauded.

He didn’t shout her name.

He didn’t need to.

For a few seconds, he watched her standing beneath the lights, surrounded by the people who loved her work.

Then the members disappeared backstage.

The concert was over.

And he was about to see his girlfriend.

Backstage, CC was halfway through removing her earrings when P’Nicha appeared at the dressing-room door.

“You’re not leaving yet.”

CC looked up.

“Why?”

“Someone is here.”

“Who?”

P’Nicha gave her a suspiciously innocent expression.

CC narrowed her eyes.

“P’Nicha.”

“What?”

“Who?”

“Go and see.”

CC stared at her manager for another moment before setting the earring down.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

“Did the company need me?”

“No.”

“Then—”

“CC.” Nicha smiled. “Just go.”

CC stood, pulling her cardigan over her stage outfit.

She stepped into the corridor, still holding her phone.

A few staff members passed by, congratulating her on the performance. She thanked them, bowing slightly, before turning into the small waiting room at the end of the corridor, which Nicha had emptied.

Then she saw him.

Declan stood near the window, speaking with Alexander.

He had changed into a charcoal suit, his jacket unbuttoned, his tie slightly loosened. One hand rested in his trouser pocket.

He looked entirely at home among the folding chairs and garment rails.

CC stopped.

Declan turned.

His face changed immediately.

Not dramatically. Just a subtle easing around his eyes, followed by the familiar smile that seemed to belong exclusively to her.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

CC blinked.

Then she looked towards Alexander.

Alexander offered a polite nod.

“Good evening, Miss Chanya.”

Then he stepped out and closed the door behind him.

She looked back at Declan.

“You’re here?”

“I am.”

“In Bangkok?”

“That’s generally where this building is.”

She gave him a look.

His smile widened slightly.

“I thought you had meetings.”

“I did.”

“And dinner?”

“I had dinner.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I wanted to surprise you.”

CC looked at him for another second before walking closer.

“You came to the concert?”

“I did.”

Her face softened.

“You watched?”

“Every minute.”

She looked almost embarrassed.

“Even the waiting part?”

“Especially the waiting part.”

“Why?”

“You were entertaining.”

She fought a smile and lost.

Then she reached him.

Declan opened his arms, and she stepped into them without hesitation.

He held her carefully, mindful of the stage outfit. One hand settled between her shoulder blades while the other rested lightly against the back of her head.

She smelled of perfume, hairspray, and the warm, familiar scent of her skin.

He lowered his head.

“You were wonderful.”

CC’s cheek rested against his chest.

“Thank you.”

“I mean it.”

“I can tell.”

He kissed the top of her head.

For a few seconds, neither spoke.

Then she tilted her face upwards.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Really?”

“Cela.”

His voice was low, amused.

“I rearranged my weekend to be here. I would hope you believe I enjoyed it.”

She laughed.

“You could have told me.”

“And lost the opportunity to see your face when you found me?”

She looked away.

“I wasn’t that surprised.”

“You stopped walking.”

“I was thinking.”

“About what?”

“Whether you were real.”

He looked down at her.

Then, with a faint smile, he said, “I can assure you I am.”

She laughed again, and he brushed his thumb lightly along her cheek.

He had seen her smiling on a screen earlier that week. He had replayed a little dance more times than he intended to admit.

But this was better.

Much better.

They were given a private room to rest before CC left.

Her stylist came in to help remove the remaining accessories, while Nicha reviewed the departure arrangements with Alexander.

Declan sat on the sofa, watching CC take off her stage earrings.

She caught his gaze in the mirror.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“I am.”

She turned slightly.

“Why?”

“Because you’re there.”

Her face changed.

It was such a simple answer that she didn’t immediately know what to say.

She looked back at the mirror, hiding a smile.

After the stylist left, she walked over to him.

“Do I look strange?”

He looked up.

She was still wearing her stage outfit, though the elaborate accessories had been removed. Her makeup was intact, but her hair had begun to loosen around her face.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Very.”

She studied his expression.

“You’re biased.”

“Extremely.”

She laughed and sat beside him.

He adjusted the cardigan around her shoulders.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Hungry?”

She turned towards him.

He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s a yes.”

“Maybe.”

“I’ve arranged for dinner.”

Her eyes brightened.

“What did you get?”

“Mango sticky rice.”

She looked delighted.

“And?”

“Several other things. I asked Nicha what you might want.”

CC turned towards the door, where her manager was standing with Alexander.

“P’Nicha!”

Nicha looked over.

“What?”

“You told him?”

“I didn’t tell him anything. I merely prevented him from ordering food you wouldn’t eat.”

Declan looked mildly amused.

“I appreciate the assistance.”

Nicha gave him a knowing smile.

“She forgets after shows. I’ve been feeding her for five years.”

CC looked between them.

“I eat.”

“Yes,” Nicha replied. “When someone reminds you.”

Declan’s expression remained composed, but the amusement in his eyes was unmistakable.

CC turned back to him.

“Don’t listen to her.”

“Of course not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I wouldn’t dream of taking sides.”

She made a face at him.

He leaned closer.

“Although I did notice you told the audience not to forget to eat.”

Her eyes widened.

“You heard that?”

“I did.”

“It’s a normal thing to say.”

“Certainly.”

“And the question about what I was eating was not—”

“An indication that you were hungry?”

She studied his face.

He looked back, entirely serious.

Then she laughed and lightly pushed his arm.

“You’re teasing me.”

“Only a little.”

He caught her hand before she could withdraw it and brought her knuckles to his lips.

“Come on, sweetheart. Let’s get you home.”

They left the arena ten minutes apart, CC in the company van and Declan in his own car, and the covered side entrance of her building did the rest.

The apartment was quiet when they arrived. CC had changed in the van into a soft cream-coloured lounge set. Her hair was now loose, and she had removed the remaining makeup with the help of a cleansing wipe.

Declan had taken off his jacket and rolled his sleeves to his forearms.

The food was arranged on the dining table.

CC stood in front of it, looking pleased.

“You ordered too much.”

“I was advised that you might be hungry.”

“P’Nicha.”

“She was quite persuasive.”

CC sat down and lifted the lid of the mango sticky rice container.

Declan watched her take the first bite.

Her eyes closed.

He smiled.

“Good?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He sat opposite her, helping himself to the other dishes.

For a while, they ate and talked about the concert. CC told him about a small mistake during rehearsal, the member who had nearly forgotten a costume change, and how the technical delay had happened because one of the stage screens needed to be reset.

Declan listened.

He asked questions, not because he needed to know the technical details, but because he liked hearing her talk about her work.

Eventually, CC put down her spoon.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Which part did you like most?”

He considered the question.

“The final song.”

“Why?”

“You looked happy.”

She lowered her eyes to the table.

“That was a nice part.”

“I also liked the technical delay.”

She looked up.

“Why?”

“You were talking to the audience.”

She smiled.

“I didn’t know what else to do.”

“You didn’t seem particularly worried.”

“The crew were working. There wasn’t much I could do.”

“You made them laugh.”

She tilted her head.

“They were being nice.”

“They were responding to you.”

She looked at him, then reached for her water.

“Did you think I was different?”

“Different from what?”

“From how I am normally.”

Declan leaned back slightly.

He understood what she was asking.

“Onstage?”

She nodded.

He considered her carefully.

“Yes.”

Her face became a little uncertain.

“Different how?”

“More expansive, perhaps. You’re quieter when we’re alone. Onstage, you give people a version of yourself that is still genuine, but much larger.”

She listened.

“And you seem very comfortable there,” he continued. “Not because you’re never nervous, but because you know what you’re doing.”

CC looked down at her hands.

“I used to be more nervous.”

“I imagine.”

“Sometimes I still am.”

“I know.”

She looked up.

“How?”

“You hold the microphone with both hands for the first song. After that, one.”

She stared at him. Nobody had ever told her that.

He covered her hand.

“But I don’t think you need to be the same person in every room,” he said. “You can be the woman who stands in front of thousands of people and performs beautifully. You can also be the woman who asks me whether we’ve ordered enough dinner.”

CC laughed.

“Those are both important roles.”

“I’m aware.”

She moved her hand beneath his, letting their fingers settle together.

“I was happy when I saw you.”

“I noticed.”

“You did?”

“You looked towards the side entrance twice.”

Her mouth fell open.

“You saw that?”

“I was watching you.”

She gave him an embarrassed smile.

“I didn’t know you were there.”

“That was the idea.”

“I think I was looking because I thought P’Nicha was supposed to tell me something.”

“Then I’m grateful she didn’t.”

CC laughed.

Declan lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“I liked seeing you from there,” he said.

“From where?”

“The audience.”

Her eyes went to his.

“Why?”

“Because I know you as my girlfriend. I see you when you’re tired, when you’re happy, when you’re deciding what to eat, when you’re trying to convince me that you don’t need another dessert.”

“I don’t do that.”

“You do.”

She smiled.

“But tonight I saw the part of your life that existed before I came into it. The people who have supported you, the work you’ve done, the happiness you give them.”

His thumb moved gently over her knuckles.

“It was nice to see.”

CC was quiet.

Then she said, “I’m glad you came.”

“So am I.”

“Next time, tell me.”

“Next time?”

She nodded.

“I want to know you’re there. Then I can look for you.”

Something in his face softened.

He brought her hand to his lips once more.

“Then next time, I’ll make sure you know.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

Later, after they had put the food away, CC returned from the bedroom carrying her phone.

Declan was sitting on the sofa, reading a message from Alexander.

She stopped in front of him.

“Can I see something?”

He looked up.

“Of course.”

She sat beside him and opened the concert recording someone from the company had already sent her.

She moved through the video until she found the moment when the technical delay had happened.

Then she turned the screen towards him.

“Look.”

He watched.

On the screen, she stood under the lights, smiling into the audience.

“Should we talk while they fix it?”

The crowd screamed.

Declan looked at her.

“You’re showing me my favourite part?”

She smiled.

“You said you liked it.”

“I did.”

She moved closer, resting her head against his shoulder.

“Then you can watch it again.”

He looked down at her.

“Is this permission?”

“Yes.”

“Very generous.”

She laughed.

He took the phone from her and set it on the table.

Then he turned towards her, drawing her gently into his arms.

“Thank you for tonight, Cela.”

She looked up.

“For what?”

“For letting me see you.”

Her smile became smaller, warmer.

“You moved your whole weekend, sat through three hours of screaming, and you’re thanking me?”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Every minute of it.”

She reached up and touched his jaw.

“I’m happy you’re here.”

He bent and kissed her.

It was a quiet kiss, without hurry. When he drew back, she remained close, her hand still resting against his cheek.

His gaze held hers.

“It’s late, and you’ve had a long night. May I stay?”

She nodded.

“I’d like that.”

He kissed her forehead.

“Then I’ll stay.”

CC settled against him, her cheek resting over his chest. Declan wrapped an arm around her, his hand resting comfortably at her waist.

Outside, Bangkok continued its usual restless movement. Cars passed below the apartment, distant voices rose and faded, and somewhere in the city, thousands of people were probably still talking about the concert.

Inside, CC was already growing sleepy.

Declan looked down at her.

“Cela?”

“Mm?”

“Next time, I want a seat closer to the stage.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

“So I can see your expressions properly.”

She smiled.

“You could come backstage.”

“I could.”

“Then you wouldn’t need a ticket.”

He considered that.

“A reasonable proposal.”

She settled back against him.

A moment passed.

Then she murmured, “But I like knowing you’re watching from the audience.”

Declan looked down at her, his expression quiet.

“Then that’s where I’ll be.”

She smiled against his shirt.

And he held her a little closer, thinking that he had spent much of his life being the person people watched when he entered a room.

Tonight, for once, he had been perfectly content to sit in the dark and watch someone else shine.
